The facility does not require a resident to give the facility control of funds as a condition of admission or stay. A resident who handles his or her own money keeps the right to do so unless a legal representative has authority.
If a resident asks the facility to hold or handle funds, the Administrator obtains a signed written delegation that states the scope of the authority and how to end it, and places it in the record.

The business office opens a separate ledger for each resident whose funds the facility holds. Resident money is kept apart from facility money and in a secure place, never in the general operating account.
For each deposit or withdrawal, staff record the date, amount, purpose and balance in the ledger. A second staff member or the Administrator verifies and signs withdrawals above [AMOUNT] .
The business office issues a written receipt for any payment or deposit on request, and gives the resident a copy of each receipt for money handled for the resident.

At least quarterly, and any time the resident asks, the business office gives the resident or representative a written accounting of receipts, expenditures and balance. Staff record the date of delivery and the recipient.
For STAR+PLUS residents, the business office keeps member trust fund records for any funds held, in the form the STAR+PLUS Handbook requires, and keeps them available for MCO and HHSC review.
The business office keeps a simple financial record of resident charges and payments, and makes it available to HHSC on request.
When a resident is discharged or dies, the business office reconciles the ledger within [NUMBER] days and returns funds to the resident, legal representative or estate, with a signed receipt.

At admission, staff offer each resident a locked area in the living quarters, record the choice, and give the resident the key or combination. Staff may not keep a master key to the locked area unless the resident agrees in writing for emergency access.

Staff help the resident make an inventory of valuable personal items at admission and whenever items are added or removed, and the resident signs the list. Items are photographed with the resident's consent.

If a resident reports missing money or property, staff notify the Administrator immediately. The Administrator searches, interviews staff and documents the outcome. Suspected theft is treated as possible exploitation and reported under SAF-01.
Staff may not borrow, buy from, sell to, accept gifts or loans from, or act as the agent for a resident in financial matters. Violations are handled under STF-07.
The Administrator reviews resident fund ledgers and trust records at least quarterly for accuracy and reports the results to the quality assurance committee (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Oversees funds handling, obtains delegations, reviews ledgers and investigates missing funds.
Keep ledgers, receipts and quarterly accountings; segregate resident funds.
Protect resident property; never take, borrow or manage resident money outside the process; report concerns.

documentation: Resident funds management choice and written delegation
Individual resident ledgers and receipts
Quarterly accountings with proof of delivery
STAR+PLUS member trust fund records
Personal property inventory and missing-property reports
Final reconciliation at discharge or death

policies.title: Advance Directives
policies.applies_to: Administrator, nursing and care staff, admissions staff; all residents and legal representatives
federal: 42 CFR 489.102 (federal advance directive requirements for Medicare and Medicaid provider types; the facility's obligations as an assisted living facility arise under Texas rule)
policies.purpose: To make sure residents are told about their right to make advance directives, that the facility's position is stated in writing, and that directives are kept and followed.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written policy on implementing advance directives, including a clear statement of any procedure the facility is unwilling or unable to provide or withhold. The facility gives each resident written notice of that policy at admission. If the resident is incapacitated, notice goes in this order of preference: the guardian; the person responsible for the resident's health care decisions; the spouse; an adult child; a parent; the person admitting the resident. If the resident later becomes able to receive it, the facility gives notice again. Residents may execute an advance directive under Texas Health and Safety Code Chapter 166. The facility keeps any advance directive in the resident record. Failure to inform residents can result in a $500 administrative penalty from HHSC, and the facility has 20 days to consent to the penalty or request a hearing. The facility does not require or prohibit an advance directive as a condition of admission.

definitions.definition: A written instruction, such as a directive to physicians, out-of-hospital DNR order or medical power of attorney, that states a person's health care wishes or names a person to decide.
Lacking the ability to understand and communicate health care decisions.
A physician-signed order directing emergency personnel not to start certain resuscitation measures.
A document naming an agent to make health care decisions for a person who cannot.

procedures: The Administrator maintains the written advance directive policy, including a clear statement of any procedure the facility is unwilling or unable to provide or withhold. The Administrator reviews it annually and when rules change (see GOV-03).
At admission, the admitting staff member gives the resident the written advance directive notice and policy, explains them in plain language, and answers questions.

If the resident appears incapacitated, staff determine and record who is the appropriate person to notify, in order: guardian; person responsible for health care decisions; spouse; adult child; parent; person admitting the resident. Staff give the notice to the highest-ranking available person.
Staff ask whether the resident has an advance directive, and record yes or no and the date. Staff do not pressure the resident to sign or not sign one, and do not make admission depend on it.

If the resident has an advance directive, staff ask for a copy, place it in the resident record where it can be found quickly, and note its location on the face sheet and the emergency information sheet.

If the resident wants to make an advance directive, staff give information, help the resident contact his or her physician, attorney or family, and ensure the resident's own physician has a copy. Staff do not act as witnesses or give legal advice.

The Nurse or Administrator ensures that an out-of-hospital DNR order, if present, is signed by the physician, is readily available (such as in the resident's room or file as directed) and is known to all shifts.
Staff review the advance directive at each reassessment and at each significant change in the resident's condition (see ADM-02), and update records and the service plan.
If the resident regains capacity, staff give the written notice again and offer to review the directive, and record the date.

In an emergency, staff follow the resident's valid directive and physician orders. If staff are unsure about the status of a directive, they call 911, begin care consistent with the facility's emergency procedures, and notify the physician and responsible person at once (see HCS-05).

If the facility is unwilling or unable to carry out a particular wish, the Administrator tells the resident or representative in writing before admission or as soon as the issue arises, and helps arrange a transfer if the resident wishes.
The Administrator keeps proof of each notice (signature, date, and recipient, or the reason a notice was given to a person other than the resident) in the resident record.
Staff are trained at orientation and annually on advance directives, DNR orders and the facility policy (see STF-03).
If HHSC proposes a $500 penalty for failure to inform a resident, the Administrator notes the deadline, and within 20 days either consents or requests a hearing, and documents the decision.
The Administrator audits resident records at least annually to confirm every record shows the notice and any directive, and corrects gaps immediately.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the written policy and statement of procedures the facility will not provide or withhold; ensures notice is given; responds to any HHSC penalty within 20 days.
Give notice, ask about directives, file copies and make them available in an emergency.
Know where directives are kept and follow the resident's directive and physician orders; escalate unclear situations.

documentation: Signed advance directive notice acknowledgment or notice to a surrogate in the order required
Copy of the resident's advance directive or documented absence
Out-of-hospital DNR order, if any
Reassessment notes reviewing the directive
Annual record audit; any HHSC penalty correspondence

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, volunteers and students of [AGENCY NAME]; all resident records in any form (paper, electronic, verbal, photographic)
policies.purpose: To protect the confidentiality of resident information, to make sure records are safeguarded from unauthorized use, loss or destruction, and to make sure records are available to the people and agencies entitled to see them.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] treats all resident records and information as confidential. Information is released only with the consent of the resident or legal representative, to another provider when a resident transfers, or when another law requires it. Records are available to residents, their legal representatives and HHSC. The State Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program and HHSC surveyors are entitled to access, and those disclosures are permitted. Confidentiality is a required orientation topic for all staff. To the extent [AGENCY NAME] is a HIPAA covered entity, for example because it bills Medicaid electronically, it also complies with the HIPAA Privacy Rule, the right-of-access standard and the breach notification rules. The same safeguards apply to all residents whether or not HIPAA applies.

definitions.definition: The admission form, assessments, service plan, physician orders, advance directives, physician exam, professional service documentation, guardianship papers and financial records kept for a resident.
A guardian, agent under a medical power of attorney or other person with documented legal authority to act for a resident.
A health care provider that transmits health information electronically in connection with a standard transaction, such as an electronic Medicaid claim, and is therefore subject to HIPAA.
The least amount of resident information needed to accomplish the purpose of a use or disclosure. It does not apply to treatment disclosures or to disclosures to the resident.

An unauthorized acquisition, access, use or disclosure of protected health information that is presumed reportable unless a documented risk assessment shows a low probability that the information was compromised.

procedures: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] is the Privacy Officer, or names a designee in writing. The Privacy Officer is the contact for all privacy questions, access requests and complaints.

During the 4-hour orientation and before any unsupervised resident contact, every new employee receives training on confidentiality and signs a confidentiality acknowledgement. The acknowledgement is filed in the personnel record. The Privacy Officer repeats a confidentiality refresher at least annually.

Paper records are kept in a locked cabinet or locked room. Only staff who need them for their job may access them. Charts are never left open or unattended in hallways, dining areas or on medication carts.

Electronic records require a unique user login and password. Staff may not share credentials. Screens are locked when staff step away. The Privacy Officer removes access on the day an employee leaves.

Staff access and share only the minimum information needed to do their jobs. Staff do not discuss residents in common areas, elevators, public spaces or on social media, and do not take photographs or video of residents without written consent.

Before releasing any record, the staff member confirms the identity of the requester. Staff check the guardianship papers, medical power of attorney or other authority on file when someone claims to act for a resident.

Information is released only (a) with the signed consent of the resident or legal representative, (b) to the receiving provider when the resident transfers, or (c) when another law requires or permits it. The Privacy Officer approves every release not covered by (b) and logs it.

When a resident or legal representative asks to see or get a copy of the record, the Privacy Officer provides access promptly. If the facility is a covered entity, the facility acts on the request no later than 30 days after receipt. The request and the date of response are logged.

HHSC surveyors and investigators get access to resident records on request. The person in charge notifies [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] and provides the records without delay. The facility records what was provided.

The State Ombudsman, certified ombudsmen and interns get access to resident records with resident consent or as the rule otherwise allows. HIPAA does not prevent release to the ombudsman, who is a health oversight agency. Questions are referred to the Privacy Officer, and access is not delayed while questions are resolved (see RR-03).

The Privacy Officer determines and documents annually whether [AGENCY NAME] is a HIPAA covered entity. If it is, the facility adopts and gives residents its Notice of Privacy Practices and follows 45 CFR 164.530 administrative requirements. These include a designated privacy official, training, safeguards, a complaint process and sanctions.
Residents' mail is delivered unopened. Personal care and treatment are given in privacy. Resident names, diagnoses and medications are not posted where visitors can see them.

Contractors and vendors who may see resident information, such as therapy, pharmacy or software vendors, are told of the confidentiality requirement. When the facility is a covered entity, the Privacy Officer decides whether a business associate agreement is required and keeps a copy.
Records that are past retention are destroyed by shredding or secure electronic deletion, as set out in REC-01. Records of a closed or discharged resident are never discarded early.

Any staff member who learns of a lost, stolen or improperly disclosed record reports it to the Privacy Officer immediately and no later than the end of the shift. The Privacy Officer investigates within 1 business day, takes steps to limit harm and documents the outcome.

If the facility is a covered entity and the incident is a breach, the Privacy Officer completes a written risk assessment. Notice goes to affected residents or representatives without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after discovery. HHSS and other required notices are made as set out in REC-02. Notice to HHS and the media follows 45 CFR Part 164 Subpart D.
Staff who violate this policy are subject to discipline up to and including termination, as set out in STF-07. Retaliation against anyone who reports a privacy concern is prohibited.
The Privacy Officer reviews safeguards, access lists and incident logs at least annually and reports the results to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] for the quality assurance program (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains this policy, trains staff, approves releases, handles access requests and investigates incidents.
Keep resident information confidential, access only what is needed and report suspected breaches immediately.
Provides surveyors, ombudsmen and residents access to records and records the access.
May review the record, request copies and give or withhold consent for releases.

documentation: Signed staff confidentiality acknowledgements
Resident or representative consent forms for release of information
Release and access request log
Documentation of legal representative authority, including guardianship order and letters
Privacy incident investigation and breach risk assessment records
Annual covered entity determination and safeguard review
Notice of Privacy Practices acknowledgements, if a covered entity

policies.title: Nondiscrimination, Language Access and Accessibility
policies.applies_to: All staff; all applicants, residents and their representatives; all admission, service and discharge decisions
federal: Fair Housing Act, 42 USC 3601 et seq.
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident is treated with dignity, can communicate in their own language and has equal access to the facility's services and physical space.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] treats each resident with dignity and respect regardless of race, religion, national origin, sex, age, disability, marital status or source of payment. Residents are not prohibited from speaking their native language with other residents or staff for purposes of treatment, care or services. The Residents' Bill of Rights is posted in each resident's primary language. The facility provides reasonable accommodations and modifications for residents with disabilities and takes reasonable steps to give people with limited English proficiency meaningful access. Decisions not to admit or retain a person are made only on the documented inability of the facility to meet the person's needs under ADM-01 and ADM-04, never on a protected characteristic.

definitions.definition: The language a resident prefers to use to communicate about health, care and daily life, recorded on the comprehensive assessment.
A limited ability to read, speak, write or understand English well enough to take part in services without help.
A change in a rule, policy, practice or service that gives a person with a disability an equal opportunity to use and enjoy the facility.
A structural change to a resident's living space or common areas, usually at the resident's expense where the law allows, so a person with a disability can use the space.
Whether a resident pays privately or through Medicaid or another payer.

procedures: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] is the nondiscrimination coordinator, or names a designee in writing. The coordinator receives questions, accommodation requests and discrimination complaints.

At first contact and again at admission, staff ask each applicant and representative what language they prefer for speaking and reading, and whether they need communication aids. The answer is recorded on the comprehensive assessment as primary language (see ADM-02).

When a resident has LEP, staff arrange an interpreter or translation of key documents such as the admission agreement, disclosure statement, rate schedule and Bill of Rights. Staff use a qualified bilingual employee, a telephone interpreter service or a community resource at no charge to the resident. A family member serves as interpreter only if the resident asks, and staff note this in the record.

The Residents' Bill of Rights is posted in each resident's primary language, and the same version is given to the resident and representative. The coordinator keeps translated copies for the languages of current residents.

Staff never tell or require residents to speak English with other residents or staff in connection with treatment, care or services. Staff who speak the resident's language are assigned to care where possible, and the language is noted in the service plan.

For residents who are deaf, hard of hearing, blind, have low vision or have other communication needs, staff provide auxiliary aids such as written materials, large print, reading documents aloud or a sign language interpreter. The need and the aid used are noted in the service plan.

Admission and retention decisions are made only under ADM-01, ADM-04 and ADM-05, based on whether the facility can meet the person's needs. The decision maker records the reasons. Race, religion, national origin, sex, age, disability, marital status and payment source are never a reason.

The facility does not refuse admission or retention solely because a resident receives Medicaid, and does not give Medicaid residents lesser services than private-pay residents. Differences in room type or amenities are described in the rate schedule.

A resident or applicant may ask for a reasonable accommodation or modification verbally or in writing. Staff forward the request to the coordinator on the same day. The coordinator discusses the request with the resident, decides promptly, documents the decision and the reason, and offers an alternative if the request cannot be granted as made.

The coordinator reviews the physical plant at least annually and corrects barriers, such as doors, bathrooms, ramps and signage, that keep residents with disabilities from using common areas, and logs the corrections. This review is tied to the maintenance program in DL-04.

Staff treat all residents with respect. Staff may not use slurs, stereotypes, jokes, differential treatment or exclusion from activities based on a protected characteristic. Any such conduct is reported to the coordinator and handled under STF-07.

Complaints of discrimination are handled under RR-02. The facility informs residents that they may also contact HHSC at 1-800-458-9858 and the State Long-Term Care Ombudsman, and that no one will be retaliated against for complaining.

The administrator and the manager complete continuing education that covers ADA accessibility, the Fair Housing Act and other applicable federal laws, as required for manager training, and the training certificates are kept in the personnel record.

The coordinator includes a nondiscrimination and language-access review in the annual quality assurance report (GOV-04), including interpreter use, accommodation requests and the outcomes of complaints.

responsibilities.duty: Receives requests and complaints, arranges interpreters and aids, decides accommodation requests and documents the outcomes.
Makes sure assessments record primary language, translated Bill of Rights copies are posted and staff follow this policy on every shift.
Communicate respectfully, allow residents to use their language and report needs and complaints at once.
Corrects accessibility barriers found in the annual review and approved modifications.

documentation: Primary language and communication needs recorded on the comprehensive assessment and service plan
Posted Residents' Bill of Rights in each resident's primary language
Interpreter and translation use log
Accommodation and modification requests, decisions and reasons
Annual accessibility review and corrections log
Documentation of reasons for any non-admission or discharge decision
Manager continuing education certificates

policies.title: Authorized Electronic Monitoring (AEM)
policies.applies_to: All residents, representatives, roommates, administrators, managers and direct care staff
policies.purpose: To allow a resident to use authorized electronic monitoring in their room as the Residents' Bill of Rights provides, while protecting the privacy and dignity of the resident, any roommate and others.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] permits electronic monitoring of a resident's room when a resident or the resident's representative requests it. The facility does not refuse to admit a person, and does not discharge a resident, because the person or the person's representative requested electronic monitoring. Covert (unauthorized) monitoring is not a ground for discharge. Every new and current resident receives and signs the HHSC form 'Information Regarding Authorized Electronic Monitoring', which is kept in the active clinical record. A request is made on the HHSC Request for AEM form. The HHSC Consent to AEM form is needed from every other resident in the room. The resident or representative pays all costs of the monitoring. Abuse or neglect seen on a recording is reported under the facility's abuse, neglect and exploitation reporting policy (SAF-01).

definitions.definition: The placement of an electronic monitoring device in a resident's room, with the consents required by HHSC, to monitor the room through video or audio.
The HHSC form a resident or representative submits to ask for electronic monitoring.

The HHSC form every other resident in the room must sign before monitoring begins. A roommate may give consent with conditions, such as pointing the camera away from the roommate's area or limiting audio.
A person authorized to act for a resident who lacks capacity, in the priority order the rule sets out for surrogates.
Electronic monitoring done without the notice, forms and consents this policy requires.

procedures: At or before admission, the administrator gives each new resident or representative the HHSC form 'Information Regarding Authorized Electronic Monitoring', and explains the right to request monitoring. The signed form is filed in the active clinical record.
[ADMINISTRATOR NAME] gives and obtains the same signed form from every current resident or representative, and the admission staff keep a roster showing the date each form was signed.

A request for monitoring may be made by the resident or the resident's representative. Any staff member who gets a request in any form directs the person to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] and gives the person the HHSC Request for AEM form on the same day. Staff do not discourage a request or ask why it is being made.

On receiving a completed request, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reviews it within 1 business day and logs the date. The facility does not delay or refuse admission or continued residence because of the request.

If the resident has a roommate, the administrator gives the roommate or representative the HHSC Consent to AEM form. Monitoring does not begin until each roommate has signed. The roommate may consent on conditions, such as pointing the camera away from the roommate's area or limiting audio, and the conditions are written on the form and followed.

If a roommate declines consent, the administrator tells the requester and discusses options, which may include a room change when one is available. The facility does not move or discharge a resident solely because of an AEM request.

If the resident lacks capacity to request AEM, the physician determines capacity, and the determination is documented in the record. The request is then made by a representative in the surrogate priority order in 26 TAC §553.267(d)(4)(C)(ii). The administrator records who signed and on what authority.

The resident or representative pays all costs of the equipment, installation, maintenance and removal, and any related costs. The administrator explains this in writing before installation. The facility provides a secure mount and access to power as required.

Staff post the notice required at the room entrance whenever AEM is in use. The facility also keeps the facility-wide 'Electronic Monitoring' notice posted at the main entrance at all times, whether or not any monitoring is in use.

On request from the resident or representative, staff obstruct the camera, for example by covering it or turning it away, to protect the resident's dignity during personal care. Staff respect the request every time and note any pattern of requests in the service plan.
Staff, visitors and contractors may not remove, move, disable or tamper with an authorized device, except to obstruct it on the resident's request, or when ordered by the resident or representative.

If staff learn of a camera or recording device in a room where no request, consent or notice exists, they report it to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] the same day. The administrator talks with the resident or representative about completing the AEM forms. The device is not a ground for discharge.

Staff who see or learn of abuse, neglect or exploitation on a recording report it under SAF-01, immediately and to HHSC at 1-800-458-9858 as that policy requires. The staff member does not wait for the administrator to review the recording.

If a resident or representative asks to stop monitoring, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] documents the request and the date. The resident or representative removes the equipment and the room notice is taken down.
Staff do not record or view AEM footage on behalf of the facility. Footage that is provided to the facility is handled as confidential resident information under RR-07.
[ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reviews the AEM log and the roster of signed forms at least quarterly and corrects any missing forms or notices.

responsibilities.duty: Distributes and collects the HHSC forms, manages requests and consents, keeps the notices posted and keeps the AEM log.
Refer requests promptly, obstruct the camera on request, do not tamper with devices and report suspected abuse or neglect.
Determines and documents whether a resident has capacity to request AEM.
Submits the Request for AEM form, pays the costs and obtains roommate consent.
May give, condition or refuse consent to monitoring in a shared room.

documentation: Signed HHSC 'Information Regarding Authorized Electronic Monitoring' form in the active clinical record for every resident
Request for AEM form
Consent to AEM forms from every other resident in the room, including written conditions
Physician capacity determination and record of the representative's authority
AEM request and decision log and the roster of signed information forms
Written cost agreement with the resident or representative
Photographs or description showing the entrance notice and the room notice are posted

policies.title: Pre-Admission Screening, Disclosure and Admission Criteria
policies.applies_to: Administrator, manager, admission staff, and all applicants, residents and legal representatives
policies.purpose: To make sure that [AGENCY NAME] admits only people whose needs it can meet, gives applicants the disclosures and notices Texas requires before admission and opens a complete record.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is licensed as a [TYPE A / TYPE B] assisted living facility. It does not admit or retain a resident whose needs it cannot meet and who cannot secure services from an outside resource. Facility management makes that decision with the written concurrence of the resident, physician or legal representative. Type A residents can evacuate without staff help. Type B residents may need evacuation help but may not be permanently bedfast. Before admission, the facility gives each applicant a written admission agreement, the disclosure statement and rate schedule, the Residents' Bill of Rights, the HHSC abuse hotline number, the restraint and seclusion notice, and the emergency plan or evacuation summary. If memory care is promoted, the facility also gives the Assisted Living Facility Memory Care Disclosure Statement, and HHSC Form 3641 if it is certified for Alzheimer's care.

definitions.definition: A facility whose residents can evacuate without staff help and that does not provide routine night attendance.
A facility whose residents may need help to evacuate and may need night attendance, but who may not be permanently bedfast.
The written statement the facility gives each applicant before admission that describes the services and the facility's operations. It is given with the rate schedule.
The disclosure the facility must give when it markets or promotes memory care, using the HHSC Assisted Living Facility Memory Care Disclosure Statement.
The HHSC disclosure form given by a facility or unit certified for Alzheimer's care. Certification applies to Type B facilities only.
A person or agency outside the facility, such as home health, hospice or a family caregiver, that provides services a resident needs.

procedures: When someone inquires, admission staff record the applicant's name, contact person and basic needs, and give the facility's rate schedule and a description of services. Staff do not promise admission before screening is complete.

Before admission, the administrator or a designee screens the applicant with the applicant, family or representative, the referring provider if any and the physician. The screen covers diagnoses, medications, mobility and ability to evacuate, behaviors, cognition, continence, nutrition and treatments, and the person's preferences.

The administrator decides whether the facility can meet the person's needs, including the staffing the needs would require. The decision is recorded on the screening form. Needs the facility cannot meet and that no outside resource can supply are a reason not to admit (see ADM-04).

For a Type A facility, the administrator confirms the applicant can evacuate without staff help. For a Type B facility, the administrator confirms the applicant is not permanently bedfast and that the evacuation help and night attendance the applicant needs can be provided. The reasoning is documented.
The administrator obtains the written concurrence of the resident, physician or legal representative with the decision to admit, and files it. If concurrence is not given, the person is not admitted.

Before admission, staff explain the disclosure statement and rate schedule and give both to the applicant or representative. The normal 24-hour staffing pattern is disclosed at this time. The date of delivery is recorded and signed.

Before admission, staff give the Residents' Bill of Rights and explain it, in the resident's primary language, and give written resident policies, the restraint and seclusion notice, and the emergency plan or evacuation summary. The resident or representative signs for each.

Staff give the family or representative the HHSC abuse hotline number, 1-800-458-9858, and document the date they received it. Staff also provide the facility's advance directive policy and notice as set out in RR-06.

If the facility promotes or markets memory care, staff give the HHSC Assisted Living Facility Memory Care Disclosure Statement before admission. If the facility or unit is Alzheimer's certified, staff also give HHSC Form 3641. Both are signed and dated.
The resident or representative signs the written admission agreement (see RR-04) before moving in. A copy goes to the resident and the original goes in the record.

The resident must have a physician exam within 30 days before admission or within 14 days after admission. If the transferring hospital or facility has a physical exam in the record, that exam satisfies the requirement. Staff follow up on any exam that is missing and document the effort.

At admission, staff collect and record the resident's full name, Social Security number, usual residence, sex, marital status, date and place of birth, usual occupation, emergency contacts and physician, pharmacy preference and Medicaid or Medicare number.

At admission, staff ask for the guardianship court order and letters, if there is a guardian. If they are not received, a follow-up request is made within 30 days. The requests and results are kept in the record.

For an emergency admission, the facility assesses the person and creates a service plan immediately, and continues with the admission steps in this policy as soon as possible. Respite service plans may be kept for 6 months.

If a person's needs turn out to be beyond what the facility can meet after admission, the administrator follows ADM-05 and ADM-06, including the inappropriate placement forms and the 30-day discharge timeline.
The administrator opens the resident record under REC-01 and arranges the comprehensive assessment and the service plan within 14 days of admission (see ADM-02 and ADM-03).
For a resident on STAR+PLUS HCBS, the administrator also follows ADM-07.

responsibilities.duty: Makes and documents the admission decision, obtains concurrence, gives all disclosures and notices and ensures the record is complete.
Conduct screening, collect identifying information, request guardianship papers and track the physician exam.
Provide accurate information, review and sign the agreement and disclosures, and concur in the admission.
Completes the physical exam within the required window and gives orders.

documentation: Pre-admission screening form with the admission decision and reasons
Written concurrence of the resident, physician or legal representative
Signed admission agreement, disclosure statement and rate schedule
Signed receipt for the Residents' Bill of Rights, restraint and seclusion notice, emergency plan or evacuation summary and written resident policies
Documented family receipt of the HHSC abuse hotline number
Memory Care Disclosure Statement and HHSC Form 3641, as applicable
Physician exam and the identifying information collected at admission
Guardianship order and letters, and the dated follow-up requests and results

policies.title: Resident Assessment and Reassessment
policies.applies_to: Administrator, manager, nursing staff (RN) and all staff who gather assessment information; all residents
policies.purpose: To make sure each resident has a complete, timely comprehensive assessment that drives the service plan, and that assessments are updated yearly and when the resident's condition changes significantly.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] completes a comprehensive assessment of each resident within 14 days of admission, using a facility-developed form. If required information cannot be obtained, the facility documents the attempts. The assessment is updated at least annually and on any significant change in condition. A registered nurse (RN) assesses and documents whether a task qualifies as a health maintenance activity (HMA) before personal care staff perform it without delegation, and reassesses on any change of condition, at least annually, and at least every 6 months for residents with Alzheimer's disease or related disorders or in a certified facility or unit. For STAR+PLUS HCBS members, the facility also completes the health assessment and emergency training within 3 days of admission.

definitions.definition: The facility's written assessment of the resident's needs, preferences and abilities, completed within 14 days of admission and used to develop the service plan.
A major decline or improvement in a resident's physical, mental or functional condition that is not expected to resolve and that affects the care the resident needs.

A task that an RN has assessed and documented as qualifying for performance by personal care staff without delegation, because the resident or representative directs it and the condition is stable and predictable.
The process under 22 TAC Chapter 225 by which an RN delegates a nursing task that is not an HMA to trained personal care staff.

procedures: On the day of admission, the manager assigns the comprehensive assessment to the staff member responsible, with the RN for nursing-related items, and records the due date, which is no later than 14 days after admission.

The assessor uses the facility's assessment form and gathers information from the resident, representative, physician, records from the prior setting and direct observation. Information that cannot be obtained is documented with the attempts made and the dates.

The assessment records the admitting location, primary language, sleep patterns, behaviors, psychosocial status and depression screen, Alzheimer's or related disorder history, ADL patterns, activity preferences, cognition and communication.

The assessment records physical function, continence, nutrition, oral and dental status, diagnoses, medications and how each is given (administered, supervised or self-administered), health conditions and medication side effects, special treatments, and hospital admissions in the past 6 months.
The assessment also identifies the resident's preventive health needs. Information gathered here feeds the fall, skin and other risk plans (HCS-07 and HCS-08).
The assessor signs and dates the assessment and gives it to the administrator, who reviews it and uses it to prepare the service plan under ADM-03 within the same 14-day period.

If a resident may need a task to be done by personal care staff that is a health maintenance activity, the RN assesses and documents in the record whether it qualifies. The resident or representative must direct the task and agree in writing, and the condition must be stable and predictable.
If the RN finds a task does not qualify as an HMA, personal care staff do not perform it unless the RN delegates it under 22 TAC Chapter 225 as set out in HCS-04.

The RN reassesses each HMA upon any change of condition and at least annually. For residents with Alzheimer's or related disorders, and for any resident in a certified facility or unit, the RN reassesses at least every 6 months. The manager keeps a tickler of due dates.

Staff report any significant change in a resident's condition to the manager and the RN on the same shift. The RN or manager completes a reassessment of the affected areas promptly, notifies the physician and representative under HCS-05 and updates the service plan.
The full comprehensive assessment is repeated at least annually, no later than the anniversary of the previous assessment. The manager sets the due dates and reviews the list monthly.

For STAR+PLUS HCBS members, the facility completes the health assessment and emergency training within 3 days of admission, as the STAR+PLUS Handbook §§7250–7252 provide. The date and trainer are documented.
The administrator reviews a sample of assessments each quarter for completeness and timeliness and reports results to the quality assurance program (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures assessments are completed on time, reviews them and uses them to set staffing and services.
Assigns assessments, tracks due dates and triggers reassessment after significant change.
Assesses nursing-related items, determines whether a task qualifies as an HMA, reassesses on schedule and delegates tasks that are not HMAs.
Observe and report changes in condition, and contribute information for assessments.

documentation: Comprehensive assessment on the facility's form, with the assessor's signature and date
Documentation of attempts to obtain unavailable information
RN HMA assessments, written agreements of the resident or representative and reassessment dates
Annual and change-of-condition reassessments
STAR+PLUS health assessment and emergency training record, where applicable
Assessment due-date tracking log and quarterly audit results

policies.title: Individual Service Plan
policies.applies_to: Administrator, manager, RN, direct care staff, residents, legal representatives and outside resource providers
policies.purpose: To make sure that each resident has a written individual service plan, built from the comprehensive assessment and approved by the resident, that guides daily care and staffing.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] completes a service plan for each resident within 14 days of admission, based on the comprehensive assessment. The resident, or the person responsible for the resident's health care decisions, approves and signs the plan, and the facility provides care according to it. The resident may participate in developing the plan. The plan is updated annually and when the resident's condition changes significantly. Staffing ratios are based on the needs identified in residents' service plans. For STAR+PLUS HCBS members, the facility coordinates its plan with the managed care organization (MCO) service plan.

definitions.definition: The facility's written plan that lists the care and services a resident will receive, who provides them and how often, based on the resident's assessed needs and preferences.
The resident's legal representative or other person authorized to make health care decisions when the resident cannot.
A provider outside the facility, such as home health or hospice, that gives a resident additional services.
The STAR+PLUS managed care organization that contracts with the facility and manages the member's services.

procedures: No later than 14 days after admission, the administrator or manager prepares the service plan from the completed comprehensive assessment (ADM-02). Plan due dates are tracked on the assessment log.

The plan lists each need identified in the assessment, the services and level of assistance that will be given, the staff or outside resource responsible, frequency, and the resident's preferences. It includes how medications are handled (administered, supervised or self-administered) and any HMAs or delegated tasks.

The administrator or manager meets with the resident, and the representative where appropriate, to review the draft. The resident is encouraged to take part in developing the plan and to state preferences, and the plan records those preferences.

The resident, or the person responsible for the resident's health care decisions, approves and signs the plan, and receives a copy. If the resident or representative disagrees with part of the plan, the disagreement and the resolution are documented.
Staff read the service plan before providing care and follow it. The plan is kept where direct care staff can use it, with the resident's privacy protected (see RR-07).
The administrator uses the needs shown on current service plans to decide the staffing levels and ratios needed on each shift, and adjusts the schedule when plans change (see STF-01).

When an outside resource such as home health or hospice gives services, the facility shares its disclosure statement, rate schedule and the resident's service plan with that provider. The provider supplies its own care plan and documents services given at the facility on the day provided. The manager files those notes in the record and coordinates the care plans (see HCS-09).

The plan is updated at least annually, no later than the anniversary of the previous plan, and whenever the resident has a significant change in condition. The updates follow a reassessment and the resident or representative signs the updated plan.

Staff who see a change that may call for a plan change report it to the manager the same shift. The manager decides on interim steps, and updates the plan without waiting for the annual date when the change is significant.

For a respite resident, the facility completes a service plan at admission. The respite service plan may be kept for 6 months. For an emergency admission, a service plan is created as soon as the assessment is done.

For STAR+PLUS HCBS members, the manager obtains the MCO service plan (ISP), compares it with the facility plan and reconciles differences. The manager notes the renewal cycle of the MCO plan and coordinates updates so the plans are consistent.

For STAR+PLUS members, the facility reports changes in condition or status to the MCO by the next business day, as the STAR+PLUS Handbook requires, and records the date and the person contacted (see ADM-07).

The resident has the right to refuse treatment or services. If a resident refuses a service in the plan, staff document the refusal, explain the risks, notify the physician and representative as appropriate, and note it in the plan.

Each quarter, the administrator reviews a sample of service plans for timeliness, resident or representative signature and consistency with the assessment, and reports results to the quality assurance program (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures service plans are complete, signed and used to set staffing, and reviews plans quarterly.
Prepares and updates plans, meets with residents and representatives, coordinates with outside resources and the MCO and tracks due dates.
Contributes nursing needs, HMAs and delegated tasks to the plan.
Follow the plan and report changes or refusals.
Take part in developing, approve and sign the plan.

documentation: Signed service plan within 14 days of admission and each update
Documentation of resident participation, preferences, disagreements and refusals
Records of sharing the disclosure statement, rate schedule and service plan with outside resources
Outside resource care plans and same-day service documentation
MCO service plan (ISP) comparison and reconciliation notes for STAR+PLUS members
Record of next-business-day notification to the MCO of changes
Service plan due-date log and quarterly audit results

policies.title: Retention Limits and Conditions the Facility Cannot Serve
policies.applies_to: Administrator/Manager, Nurse, direct-care staff, and admissions personnel at all [AGENCY NAME] Type A and Type B locations
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] admits and retains only residents whose care and evacuation needs it can safely meet, and to define the conditions the facility cannot serve under Texas assisted living rules.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will not admit or retain a resident whose needs cannot be met by the facility, its staffing, and its building. The facility will not provide ongoing services comparable to those of a licensed nursing facility (§553.261(c)(1)). A Type B facility will not retain a resident who is permanently bedfast (§553.5). 'Aging in place' with outside services is allowed only with the written concurrence of the resident, the physician, or the legal representative. Even then, the facility must continue to meet NFPA 101 and Subchapter D requirements for each resident's evacuation capability (§553.259(a)(1)). The facility may refuse an inappropriate referral and may maintain a weapons-free and drug-free environment (§553.267(b)(2)(H),(I)). If the building and staffing cannot meet a resident's evacuation needs, the facility follows ADM-05. If the facility will not retain the resident, it follows ADM-06.

definitions.definition: A facility whose residents can evacuate without staff help and that has no routine night attendance requirement.
A facility that may serve residents who need evacuation help and night attendance, but who may not be permanently bedfast.
A resident who is confined to bed on a continuing basis and is not expected to return to ambulation or transfer out of bed.
Continuing to serve a resident whose needs have increased by adding outside services (for example, home health or hospice) while the resident stays in the facility.
Ongoing services comparable to those of a licensed nursing facility, which an assisted living facility may not provide.
A resident's ability to leave the building in an emergency, with or without staff help, as measured against NFPA 101 and Subchapter D requirements.

procedures: Before any admission, the Administrator or designee reviews the referral, the physician information, and the pre-admission screening (ADM-01) to decide whether [AGENCY NAME] can meet the person's care and evacuation needs.

The Administrator confirms the facility's license type (Type A or Type B). The facility does not accept a person whose evacuation or night-attendance needs exceed what that license type and the building allow.

The Administrator compares the person's evacuation capability with the building's construction, fire protection systems, and the posted staffing pattern. If staffing and building cannot meet the need, the facility declines the referral or follows ADM-05.

The Administrator declines a referral that is inappropriate for the facility. This includes needs that would require ongoing nursing-facility-level services. The Administrator documents the reason and tells the referral source and the person or representative promptly.
The facility does not admit anyone who is permanently bedfast to a Type B facility. The facility does not admit anyone who needs ongoing nursing-facility-level services.
The weapons-free and drug-free environment rule is explained at admission. A prospective resident or visitor who will not comply may be refused. The Administrator documents the decision.

At each reassessment and at any change of condition (ADM-02, HCS-05), the Nurse or Administrator asks whether the resident's needs can still be met, whether evacuation capability has changed, and whether the resident is bedfast.

If the resident's needs can be met only with outside services (aging in place), the Administrator obtains written concurrence from the resident, the physician, or the legal representative before continuing the arrangement. The concurrence is filed in the resident record.
For any resident who ages in place, the Administrator confirms that the facility still meets NFPA 101 and Subchapter D requirements for that resident's evacuation capability, and records the review.
Outside services such as home health or hospice are coordinated under HCS-09. They supplement the facility's services and do not replace the facility's own duties.

If a Type B resident becomes permanently bedfast, or any resident develops needs the facility cannot meet, the Administrator starts the retention review within one business day. The Administrator notifies the physician and the resident or representative.
If the resident still meets evacuation criteria and the facility wishes to retain the resident, the Administrator follows ADM-05 and submits the required forms to HHSC on time.
If the facility will not or cannot retain the resident, the Administrator follows ADM-06 and gives 30 days' written notice, except in an emergency. The Administrator offers help with relocation.
The Administrator keeps a log of each retention review. The log records the date, the reason for the review, the decision, and the people notified. Reviews with no change are logged as well.
The Administrator reviews all retention decisions at least quarterly as part of quality assurance (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Makes admission and retention decisions, obtains written concurrence for aging in place, starts ADM-05 or ADM-06 when needed, and keeps the retention review log.
Assesses care needs and evacuation capability at admission, at reassessment, and at any change of condition, and reports findings to the Administrator and physician.
Report changes in a resident's mobility, continence, behavior, or ability to evacuate to the Nurse or Administrator the same shift.
Participate in retention discussions and give written concurrence when aging in place is proposed.

documentation: Pre-admission screening and referral decision, including reasons for any declined referral
Written concurrence for aging in place, signed by the resident, physician, or legal representative
Retention review log and evacuation-capability review notes
Physician notification and family or representative notification records
Copies of any ADM-05 or ADM-06 forms and notices

policies.title: Inappropriate Placement and Evacuation Waiver
policies.applies_to: Administrator/Manager, Nurse, and admissions personnel at all [AGENCY NAME] Type A and Type B locations
policies.purpose: To set out how [AGENCY NAME] responds when HHSC or the facility determines that a resident's placement may be inappropriate, so required forms are filed on time and the resident is kept safe.
policies.policy: When a resident's change of condition raises a question about appropriate placement, [AGENCY NAME] follows the Texas inappropriate-placement process. If the resident still meets the evacuation criteria and the facility wishes to keep the resident, the facility submits the Physician's Assessment (Form 1126), the Resident's Request to Remain (Form 1125), and the Facility Request (Form 1124) within 10 working days of receiving HHSC Form 3724 and Form 3614-A, or of the facility's own determination (§553.259(e)(1)). If the facility does not meet the evacuation requirements for a designated resident, it requests an evacuation waiver from the HHSC regional office within 10 working days. If the facility is unwilling to retain the resident, it discharges the resident within 30 days after receiving Forms 3724 and 3614-A (§553.259(e)(2)).

definitions.definition: A situation in which a resident's condition no longer fits the facility's license type or evacuation capability.
HHSC forms notifying the facility of a placement or evacuation-capability finding for a designated resident.
Physician's Assessment of the resident.
Resident's Request to Remain in the facility.
Facility Request to retain the resident.
HHSC approval, requested through the regional office, allowing the facility to keep a resident whose evacuation capability does not meet the standard.
The Fire Marshal Notification Form (1127) and the Fire Suppression Authority Notification Form (1129), included in a waiver packet.

procedures: On receiving Form 3724 and Form 3614-A from HHSC, or when the Administrator or Nurse determines that a resident may be inappropriately placed, the Administrator records the date received or determined. This date starts the 10-working-day clock and the 30-day discharge clock.

The Administrator calendars both deadlines the same day: the date 10 working days out and the date 30 days out. The Administrator notifies the resident or legal representative and the physician at once.

The Administrator, with the Nurse, decides which situation applies. In the first, the resident still meets the evacuation criteria. In the second, the facility does not meet the evacuation requirements for the resident. In the third, the facility will not retain the resident.

If the resident still meets the evacuation criteria and the facility wishes to retain the resident, the Administrator requests the Physician's Assessment (Form 1126) and asks the resident or representative to complete the Resident's Request to Remain (Form 1125).
The Administrator completes the Facility Request (Form 1124) and submits Forms 1124, 1125, and 1126 to HHSC within 10 working days. The Administrator keeps proof of submission.
If the facility does not meet the evacuation requirements for the resident, the Administrator starts an evacuation waiver request to the HHSC regional office within 10 working days.

The waiver packet contains: Forms 1126, 1125, and 1124; a detailed emergency plan (staff positions, awake night staff, and evacuation training); a floor plan; the evacuation plan; 12 months of fire drill records; Fire Marshal Notification Form 1127; Fire Suppression Authority Notification Form 1129; an assessment completed within the last 60 days; the resident's service plan; and the service plans of other residents if HHSC asks for them.
The Administrator sends Form 1127 to the local Fire Marshal and Form 1129 to the fire suppression authority. The Administrator keeps copies and delivery proof.
The Nurse makes sure the assessment is no more than 60 days old when the packet is sent. If it is older, the Nurse completes a new assessment (ADM-02) first.
The Administrator pulls the last 12 months of fire drill records (SAF-06). If drills are missing or incomplete, the Administrator corrects the gap before submission and notes the correction.

The Administrator reviews the emergency plan with the Nurse and shift staff. The plan must name staff positions and the awake night staff. Staff are trained on the resident-specific evacuation steps and the training is documented.

While the request is pending, the Administrator puts interim safeguards in place. Examples are extra checks, a room closer to an exit, or added staff at night. These are written into the service plan (ADM-03).

If the facility is unwilling to retain the resident, the Administrator starts ADM-06 and makes sure discharge occurs within 30 days after receipt of Forms 3724 and 3614-A. The Administrator coordinates relocation with the resident, family, physician, and receiving provider.
The Administrator files the final HHSC response in the resident record and updates the service plan to match any conditions HHSC sets. The Administrator briefs all staff on the changes.
The Administrator reports each inappropriate-placement matter and its outcome to the quality assurance review (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Tracks deadlines, submits Forms 1124, 1125, 1126 and any waiver packet to HHSC, sends Forms 1127 and 1129, and decides whether to retain or discharge.
Completes the current assessment, coordinates the physician's assessment, and helps write interim safeguards and the evacuation training.
Completes the Physician's Assessment (Form 1126).
Complete the Resident's Request to Remain (Form 1125) if the resident wishes to stay.
Complete evacuation training for the resident and carry out the interim safeguards.

documentation: Forms 3724 and 3614-A with date-received stamp
Forms 1124, 1125, 1126, 1127, and 1129, with proof of submission
Waiver packet copy, including emergency plan, floor plan, evacuation plan, and 12 months of fire drill records
Assessment (within 60 days) and service plan
Evacuation training roster and interim safeguards
HHSC response and any discharge notice (ADM-06)

policies.title: Discharge, Transfer and Relocation Notice
policies.applies_to: Administrator/Manager, Nurse, direct-care staff, and business office staff at all [AGENCY NAME] locations
policies.purpose: To make sure every discharge or transfer by [AGENCY NAME] is lawful, is supported by one of the permitted grounds, is made with proper written notice, and is carried out safely.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] discharges or transfers a resident only on the grounds Texas rules allow: (1) the move is for the resident's welfare and the resident's needs cannot be met; (2) the resident's health improved so the services are no longer needed; (3) the resident's health or safety, or that of another person, is endangered; (4) the provider ceases to operate or leaves the reimbursement program; or (5) the resident fails to pay after reasonable notice (§553.267(a)(3)(X)). Except in an emergency, the facility gives 30 days' written notice to the resident, legal representative, or family member. The notice states the intent to discharge, the reason, the effective date, the destination if any, and appeal rights (§553.267(a)(3)(Y)). An immediate termination because of a serious or immediate threat requires notice to HHSC at 1-800-458-9858 (§553.267(b)(2)(C)). Discharge will not be based on a resident's or representative's request for electronic monitoring (§553.267(d)(2)).

definitions.definition: The end of a resident's stay with the facility, whether the resident goes home, to another facility, or elsewhere.
A move of the resident to another setting, including a hospital transfer that the facility does not expect to be temporary.
Written notice given to the resident, legal representative, or family member at least 30 days before the effective date, with the content required by rule.
A discharge made without the usual notice period because of an emergency or a serious or immediate threat to health or safety.
A person with legal authority to act for the resident, such as a guardian or agent under a power of attorney.

procedures: Before any discharge or transfer, the Administrator confirms in writing which permitted ground applies and records the facts supporting it. If no permitted ground applies, the resident is not discharged.

The Administrator reviews the facts with the Nurse and, when relevant, the physician. The Administrator confirms that the discharge is not related to any complaint, grievance, ombudsman contact, or request for electronic monitoring (RR-09).
The Administrator meets with the resident and the legal representative or family member, explains the reason, and listens to their views. The Administrator offers help finding a suitable new setting.

Except in an emergency, the Administrator prepares the 30-day written notice. The notice states the intent to discharge, the specific reason, the effective date, the destination if known, and the resident's appeal rights.

The Administrator delivers the notice to the resident, legal representative, or family member, and documents the date and method of delivery and who received it. Delivery is by hand with signature or by a traceable method.
The notice and the discussion are given in a language and format the resident can understand (RR-08). The Administrator explains that the resident may contact the ombudsman (RR-03).
If a resident is in the STAR+PLUS HCBS program, the Administrator notifies the MCO by the next business day and coordinates the move with the MCO service coordinator (ADM-07).
For a discharge because of an inappropriate placement determination, the Administrator confirms that discharge occurs within the 30-day period set out in ADM-05.

For an immediate termination because of a serious or immediate threat, the Administrator calls HHSC at 1-800-458-9858 before or at the time of the termination and records the date, time, and the HHSC contact. The Administrator then documents the facts and arranges for the resident's immediate safety, such as emergency services or a safe placement.

The Nurse prepares a transfer summary with current diagnoses, allergies, medication list, recent changes, and contact information for the physician and representative. The Nurse sends it with the resident or to the receiving provider.

Medications held in central storage are released to a discharged resident on a signed receipt, per HCS-01. The Nurse or Administrator counts and lists each medication with the resident or representative and obtains the signature.

The business office completes the final accounting under RR-04 and returns the resident's funds, deposits, and personal property as RR-05 requires. The resident or representative signs for the items returned.
On the day of discharge, the Administrator confirms the destination and the transport, and that the resident leaves with medications, belongings, and the transfer summary.
The Administrator closes the record under REC-01, keeps the notice and delivery proof, and sends any reports required under REC-02.
The Administrator reviews each discharge in the next quality assurance meeting (GOV-04) for reasons, timeliness of notice, and any trend.

responsibilities.duty: Decides on discharge, confirms the permitted ground, issues the 30-day notice, notifies HHSC and the MCO when required, and closes the record.
Prepares the transfer summary, counts and releases medications on a signed receipt, and informs the physician.
Completes the final accounting and the return of funds and deposits.
Support the resident during the move and make sure belongings are packed and inventoried.
Receive the notice, take part in planning, and sign receipts for medications and belongings.

documentation: Written statement of the permitted ground and supporting facts
30-day written notice and proof of delivery
HHSC notification record for any immediate termination (date, time, contact)
Transfer summary and medication release receipt
Final accounting and property return receipt
MCO notification record, if applicable
Discharge note in the resident record

policies.title: STAR+PLUS HCBS Assisted Living Participation
policies.applies_to: Administrator/Manager, Nurse, business office staff, and direct-care staff at any [AGENCY NAME] location that contracts with STAR+PLUS managed care organizations
policies.purpose: To set out how [AGENCY NAME] meets the operating and billing requirements that apply when it serves members of the Texas STAR+PLUS Home and Community Based Services (HCBS) program in assisted living.
policies.policy: This policy applies only to [AGENCY NAME] locations that contract with STAR+PLUS managed care organizations (MCOs). The MCO contract states which housing options the facility offers (apartment single or double, or non-apartment). Non-apartment settings are freestanding buildings licensed for 16 or fewer beds. A member lives in a facility that is contracted with the member's MCO. The facility will complete a health assessment and emergency training within 3 days of admission, offer at least 4 social activities a week, report changes to the MCO by the next business day, and keep member trust fund records (Handbook §§7250–7252). Room and board is the SSI rate minus the $85 personal needs allowance ($909 per month in 2026). It cannot be waived, but a lower amount may be accepted. It is prorated in the first month and is due on a written date. SSI recipients owe no copayment (§§7240–7241.1). The facility bills HCPCS T2031 with the level modifier on the new individual service plan (ISP) and continues to bill a member's current RUG-III code until the ISP renews, under the rate methodology effective 9/1/2025. The facility meets the federal HCBS setting standards and State screening and enrollment of managed care network providers (42 CFR 438.602).

definitions.definition: A Texas Medicaid managed care program that pays for home and community based services, including assisted living, for eligible members.
Managed care organization that contracts with the State and with the facility to provide and pay for member services.
Individual service plan used by the MCO and facility to set the member's services and the billing level.
The billing code for assisted living daily service, used with a level modifier.
The previous resource utilization group classification a member may still be billed under until the ISP renews.
The monthly amount the member pays the facility for room and meals. It equals the SSI rate minus $85 ($909 per month in 2026).
Money of a member held by the facility for the member, with records required by the Handbook.

procedures: Before accepting STAR+PLUS members, the Administrator confirms that the facility holds a current contract with each MCO whose members it will serve and that the State screening and enrollment of the facility as a managed care network provider is complete and current. The Administrator files the proof.

The Administrator reads each MCO contract and records which housing options are offered: apartment single, apartment double, or non-apartment. The Administrator offers members only the options in the contract. A non-apartment setting is used only in a freestanding building licensed for 16 or fewer beds.

Before admission, the Administrator confirms with the MCO that the member is authorized for assisted living and that the member is choosing the facility. The member is also told about the interest list at 1-877-438-5658 if the member has not yet been enrolled.
The facility completes the standard admission steps in ADM-01 and RR-04. It also states the room and board amount and the written due date in the admission agreement.
Within 3 days of admission, the Nurse completes the health assessment and trains the member on emergency procedures. Both are documented in the resident record.

The business office sets room and board at the SSI rate minus $85 ($909 per month in 2026). It does not waive room and board. If the member cannot pay the full amount, the Administrator may accept a lower amount and documents the reason. In the first month, room and board is prorated.
The business office does not charge SSI recipients any copayment. For any member with a copayment, the business office follows the Handbook and the member's authorization.
The Activities Coordinator plans and documents at least 4 social activities a week that are open to members (DL-03). Attendance and offerings are recorded weekly.

The Administrator or Nurse reports any change in a member's condition, hospital stay, move, or death to the MCO by the next business day. The report is logged with the date, time, person contacted, and reference number if any.

For any member funds the facility holds, the business office maintains trust fund records showing each deposit, expense, and balance, with receipts. The records are reconciled monthly and reviewed by the Administrator (RR-05).

The business office bills HCPCS T2031 with the level modifier set in the new ISP. For a member whose ISP has not yet renewed, the business office continues to bill the member's current RUG-III code until the ISP renews.
The business office checks each MCO remittance against the authorizations and ISP levels, and corrects any difference with the MCO promptly. Billing integrity follows GOV-05.

The Administrator reviews the facility's compliance with the HCBS setting standards. These include privacy, choice, control of personal funds and schedule, and freedom from coercion. The Administrator corrects any practice that conflicts with them (RR-01).
For a discharge or transfer of a member, the Administrator follows ADM-06 and notifies the MCO by the next business day.
The Administrator keeps current copies of the MCO contracts and the Handbook sections, and updates this policy when the rate methodology, Handbook, or contract changes (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains MCO contracts and State enrollment, decides housing options offered, oversees compliance, and reports to the MCO.
Completes the health assessment and emergency training within 3 days of admission and reports changes of condition.
Calculates and collects room and board, bills T2031 or the current RUG-III code correctly, and keeps trust fund records.
Provides and documents at least 4 social activities a week.
Authorizes services, sets the ISP, and receives the facility's reports.

documentation: MCO contracts and State screening and enrollment proof
Authorization and ISP for each member
Health assessment and emergency training record within 3 days of admission
Weekly social activity log (at least 4 per week)
MCO change notification log
Room and board calculation, proration, and any reduction approval
Member trust fund ledger, receipts, and monthly reconciliations
Billing records and MCO remittance reconciliations

policies.title: Medication Management, Storage and Disposal
policies.applies_to: Administrator/Manager, Nurse, medication aides, and all staff who handle or have access to resident medications at all [AGENCY NAME] locations
policies.purpose: To make sure all resident medications at [AGENCY NAME] are received, stored, secured, and disposed of safely and in line with Texas assisted living rules.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides a locked area for all medications: central storage, a medication cart, or the resident's room. Each resident's medications are stored separately from other residents' medications (§553.261(a)(5)). Refrigerated medications are kept in a designated locked area unless the refrigerator is inside a locked medication room. Poisons and 'external use only' items are stored separately within the locked medication area. If controlled drugs are stored, the facility prevents diversion. Discontinued and expired medications and the medications of deceased residents are kept separate from current medications and are disposed of by a Texas-licensed registered pharmacist (§553.261(a)(6)(A)). Needles and syringes are disposed of in accordance with State rules for sharps. Medications held in central storage are released to a discharged resident on a signed receipt (§553.261(a)(6)(C)). Prescriptions are dispensed by a pharmacy or the resident's treating physician or dentist. Physician samples must have specific dosage instructions for the individual resident.

definitions.definition: A locked area in which the facility keeps residents' medications, with each resident's medications stored separately.
A drug regulated under federal and State controlled substance laws, such as an opioid or benzodiazepine.
The loss, theft, or use of a medication for a purpose other than the one the prescriber ordered.
A medication the prescriber has stopped, changed, or replaced.
Needles, syringes, lancets, and similar items that can puncture skin.
A medication supplied directly by a physician at no cost. It requires specific dosage instructions for the individual resident.

procedures: The Administrator designates the locked medication storage area or areas (central storage, medication cart, or resident rooms) in writing and lists who holds keys or codes. Keys are limited to the Nurse, authorized medication staff, and the Administrator.
The Nurse checks that each resident's medications are stored separately from those of other residents, using separate bins, bags, or drawers labeled with the resident's name.

When a medication arrives, a staff member authorized under HCS-02 checks it against the order and the pharmacy label. The staff member records the receipt in the resident's medication profile and puts the medication in locked storage at once.

Prescriptions are accepted only if dispensed by a pharmacy or by the resident's treating physician or dentist. A physician sample is accepted only with specific dosage instructions written for that resident. If the instructions are missing, the Nurse contacts the physician before the sample is used.

Refrigerated medications are kept in a designated locked area. If the refrigerator is not inside a locked medication room, it is locked or the medications are kept in a locked box inside it. The Nurse records the refrigerator temperature daily and reports readings outside the manufacturer's range to the pharmacist.
Poisons and 'external use only' products are stored separately from oral and injectable medications within the locked medication area, and are labeled.

If the facility stores controlled drugs, the Nurse keeps them under double lock or in a locked compartment and counts them with a second authorized staff person at each shift change. The count is recorded on a controlled drug log that both persons sign.

A missing or unexplained difference in a controlled drug count is reported to the Nurse and Administrator at once. The Administrator investigates, notifies the physician and pharmacy, and reports to law enforcement and other authorities as required (SAF-02, REC-02).

Medications that are discontinued or expired, and those of a deceased resident, are removed from the active supply at once. They are labeled and kept in a locked area separate from current medications.

A Texas-licensed registered pharmacist disposes of discontinued, expired, and deceased residents' medications. The Nurse lists each item, quantity, and date. The pharmacist signs the disposal record. Staff do not flush, discard in trash, or give away resident medications.
Needles, syringes, and other sharps are placed in a puncture-resistant sharps container and disposed of according to State sharps rules. Containers are replaced when about three-quarters full.

When a resident is discharged, the Nurse releases medications held in central storage to the resident or representative. The Nurse lists each medication and quantity and obtains a signed receipt (ADM-06).
The Nurse inspects all medication storage areas monthly for expired items, labeling, separation, temperature, and security. The Nurse records the findings and corrective actions.
If a key or code is lost or an unauthorized person may have had access, the Administrator re-keys or changes the code the same day and reviews for missing medications.
The Administrator reviews the monthly inspection records at the quality assurance meeting (GOV-04) and corrects any recurring problem.

responsibilities.duty: Designates storage areas and key holders, investigates losses, and makes sure disposal is carried out by a licensed pharmacist.
Oversees receipt, storage, counts, monthly inspection, disposal, and release of medications at discharge.

responsibilities.role: Medication staff (licensed nurse, permitted medication aide, or RN-delegated employee)
responsibilities.duty: Check medications at receipt, store them securely, and report discrepancies at once.
Disposes of discontinued, expired, and deceased residents' medications and signs the disposal record.
