The staff member completes an incident report the same shift (SAF-02) describing the events before the emergency, the less restrictive measures tried, the restraint used, the duration, the resident's condition and the notifications made.

The Manager reassesses the resident within [PERIOD] after any restraint use, reviews the triggers for the behavior and updates the service plan to avoid future use (ADM-02, ADM-03). If the facility cannot safely serve the resident, the Administrator follows ADM-04.

At orientation and in annual training, the Manager trains all direct-care staff on behavior management, de-escalation, practices to decrease restraint use and alternatives to restraint (STF-03). Training is recorded in the personnel file.
Residents may complain about restraint without reprisal. Staff direct complaints to the Manager and Administrator and follow RR-02. Suspected misuse of restraint as abuse is reported under SAF-01.
The Administrator reviews every use of restraint at the quality assurance meeting (GOV-04) to confirm that the rules were followed and to identify ways to reduce use.

The Administrator reads the full text of 26 TAC §553.261(g) on restraints and seclusion at each annual policy review (GOV-03) and updates this policy and staff training so that they match the current rule text.

responsibilities.duty: Prohibits restraint for discipline or convenience, ensures training, reviews each use, and keeps this policy current with the rule text.
Gives the restraint notice at admission, obtains and files physician authorizations and guardian consent, and updates service plans.
Use alternatives first, apply restraint only as authorized or in an emergency, and document and report each use.
Provides written authorization stating the circumstances and duration, and reviews the need for continued use.

documentation: Signed notice of restraint and seclusion policy
Written physician authorization stating circumstances and duration
Guardian informed consent where required
Incident report for each emergency use
Notification log
Training records on behavior management and alternatives
Quality assurance review of restraint use

policies.title: Emergency Preparedness and Disaster Plan
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Administrator, the Emergency Preparedness Coordinator and the alternate, residents and their representatives
policies.purpose: To ensure [AGENCY NAME] can protect residents before, during and after an emergency by keeping a documented risk assessment and a written plan that is coordinated with local emergency management and shared with residents and representatives.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written emergency preparedness plan based on a documented risk assessment. The plan covers the eight core functions: direction and control, warning, communication, sheltering, evacuation, transportation, health and medical needs, and resource management. The facility names an Emergency Preparedness Coordinator and an alternate. It coordinates with the local Emergency Management Coordinator (EMC), registers with 2-1-1 Texas, and gives every resident and representative the plan or an evacuation summary at admission. When the facility shelters in place, it keeps indoor temperatures between 68°F and 82°F. When it decides to shelter or evacuate, it notifies the HHSC regional office and the EMC immediately. The plan is reviewed at least annually and within 30 days after an event, a drill shortcoming or a rule change. Facility staff will review the full text of 26 TAC §553.275, including the parts on staff accompaniment, training, drills and return of residents, at each annual review and confirm the plan reflects it.

definitions.definition: The staff member designated in writing to develop, maintain and direct the emergency plan. An alternate is also designated.
The local government official responsible for emergency management in the facility's city or county.
Keeping residents inside the facility during an emergency because evacuation is unnecessary or unsafe.
A licensed facility that has agreed in writing to accept [AGENCY NAME]'s residents if the facility evacuates.
The state information and referral network used to register for evacuation assistance.

procedures: The Administrator designates an Emergency Preparedness Coordinator and an alternate in writing, records their names and phone numbers in the plan, and updates them within 5 days of any change.

The EPC completes and dates a written risk assessment at least annually. It covers fire, power outage, water contamination, wildfire, hazardous materials, active shooter or bomb threat, flood, hurricane or severe weather, epidemic or pandemic, cyber attack and loss of the facility.

The EPC writes or updates the plan so that it addresses all eight core functions: direction and control, warning, communication, sheltering, evacuation, transportation, health and medical needs, and resource management. The plan names who does what on each shift, including nights and weekends.
The EPC records the name and contact information of the local EMC, notifies the EMC of the facility's plan, and documents each coordination contact (date, person, topic).
The EPC keeps a printed copy of the plan in [LOCATION OF CENTRAL BINDER] where staff, residents and representatives can reach it at any time.

At admission, the admissions staff member gives the resident and representative the plan or an evacuation summary, and obtains a signed acknowledgment that is filed in the resident record. The facility provides the plan again on request and when a resident's condition changes significantly.

The EPC registers the facility with 2-1-1 Texas and re-verifies the registration annually. Staff tell residents and representatives how to register for evacuation assistance, and document that conversation at admission.

For sheltering in place, the plan lists the sources of safe power, backup power and cooling or heating. The Administrator or the person in charge checks and records indoor temperatures on [TEMPERATURE LOG] at least every [INTERVAL] hours, and acts to keep them between 68°F and 82°F. If that cannot be done, the facility moves residents to a safe location.

The Administrator or EPC makes the decision to shelter or evacuate. Immediately after deciding, the EPC notifies the HHSC regional office and the EMC. The facility records the time, the person notified and the person who made the notification.

The facility evacuates whenever the county judge or mayor orders an evacuation. The plan names a pre-arranged destination and a receiving facility, and the EPC holds a written acknowledgment from that facility and from an alternate facility. The EPC reviews both acknowledgments at least annually.

Transportation arrangements for evacuation are set out in the plan and coordinated under DL-05. They state the vehicles, drivers and number of residents who need assistance, and are adjusted as the resident census changes.
The plan covers pets and service animals living at the facility: carriers, food and records, and who is responsible for them during sheltering or evacuation.

The plan provides for health and medical needs. During an emergency, the nurse or the person in charge makes sure each resident has the following with them: medications and the medication record, physician and contact information, diet orders and any equipment, and an identification band or card.

The EPC trains all staff on their emergency roles at orientation and thereafter at least annually, and runs drills as required by the rules. The EPC documents attendance and writes down any shortcoming found in a drill.

The EPC reviews and updates the plan at least annually and within 30 days after any emergency event, drill shortcoming or rule change. The Administrator signs and dates each revision, and the old version is kept for reference.
After an emergency, the EPC debriefs staff within 7 days, records lessons learned, and reports as required under REC-02.

responsibilities.duty: Designates the EPC and alternate, approves the plan, makes or confirms the shelter or evacuate decision, and ensures resources are available.
Maintains the risk assessment and plan, coordinates with the EMC and receiving facilities, handles 2-1-1 registration, notifies HHSC and the EMC, runs training and drills, and leads reviews.
Give the plan or evacuation summary at admission and file the signed acknowledgment.
Know their emergency role, follow the plan and help residents shelter or evacuate.

documentation: Annual risk assessment
Written emergency plan and revision history
EPC and alternate designation
EMC contact information and coordination log
Written acknowledgments from the receiving facility and alternate
2-1-1 Texas registration confirmation
Signed resident or representative acknowledgment of the plan or evacuation summary
Temperature logs during sheltering
Records of HHSC and EMC notifications
Drill and training records and post-event debriefs

policies.title: Fire Safety, Evacuation and Drills
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Administrator, the maintenance person and contracted fire-system vendors
policies.purpose: To keep the building's fire protection systems working, ensure residents can be evacuated safely given their evacuation capability, and train staff through documented drills.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains fire protection and life safety systems as required by 26 TAC Subchapter D and NFPA 101. A new small Type A or Type B facility has an NFPA 13, 13R or 13D sprinkler system selected under NFPA 101 with electrical supervision, and a manual fire alarm with smoke detection. The facility admits and retains only residents whose evacuation capability matches its license type (Type A residents can evacuate without staff help; Type B residents may need evacuation help). It keeps staff sufficient to evacuate residents safely. It conducts and documents fire drills and keeps the records, and it trains every employee on emergency and evacuation procedures at orientation. The Administrator will confirm the required drill frequency from Subchapter D and the unread parts of 26 TAC §553.275 and record it in the drill schedule.

definitions.definition: A resident's ability to get out of the building safely, either without help (Type A) or with staff help (Type B).
A practice evacuation or response that tests staff and residents, with timing and results recorded.
Monitoring that signals a fault in the sprinkler or alarm system.

procedures: Before licensure and whenever the building is altered, the Administrator confirms with the licensing and survey process that the building meets the Subchapter D requirements for its size and type, including the sprinkler system (NFPA 13, 13R or 13D, as selected) with electrical supervision for a new small Type A or Type B facility.

The facility maintains a manual fire alarm system with a whole-building evacuation alarm. Smoke detectors are installed in bedrooms, corridors, living and dining rooms, offices, kitchens, laundries and common areas, on a dedicated circuit with secondary power, as required under NFPA 72.

The maintenance person visually checks exit paths, exit doors, extinguishers and alarm panel status [FREQUENCY, e.g., weekly], and logs the checks on [FIRE SAFETY CHECKLIST]. Any defect is reported to the Administrator the same day and corrected promptly, with interim protection for residents if a system is out of service.

The Administrator contracts with a qualified vendor for inspection and testing of the sprinkler and alarm systems and extinguishers at the intervals the code requires, and files each inspection report.
The facility's evacuation plan for each shift, with exit routes and assembly points, is posted. The Administrator or designee reviews it with each new employee.

At orientation (the 4-hour orientation required for all staff), the trainer covers emergency and evacuation procedures, including alarm response, resident assistance, extinguisher use and the assembly point. Attendance is documented.

The Administrator establishes a drill schedule that covers every shift, including nights. It meets the frequency required by Subchapter D and the emergency preparedness rule, and the Administrator confirms that frequency at each annual review.

During each drill the person leading it records the date, time, shift, type of drill, number of staff and residents participating, time to evacuate, problems found and corrective action, and signs the record.

The Administrator reviews drill results within 7 days. If a shortcoming is found, the Administrator corrects it, retrains staff, repeats the drill if needed, and notifies the EPC, who updates the emergency plan within 30 days.

At admission and at each reassessment, the nurse or Administrator determines each resident's evacuation capability and documents it in the assessment (see ADM-02) and in the service plan. A resident whose capability exceeds the facility's license type is handled under ADM-04 and ADM-05.

If a resident's evacuation capability changes, the Administrator completes the Fire Marshal notification (Form 1127) and the Fire Suppression notification (Form 1129), as required, sends them the same day the change is identified, and files copies.

Staffing is kept at levels sufficient to safely evacuate residents, including at night (see STF-01). The Administrator reviews the staffing pattern against the evacuation capability of current residents whenever the census or resident mix changes.

If HHSC requires an evacuation waiver for an inappropriate placement, the Administrator provides fire drill records for the last 12 months on request. The facility therefore keeps drill records for at least 12 months and longer where its retention schedule requires.

In a fire, staff follow the posted procedure: rescue residents in immediate danger, sound the alarm, call 911, close doors, evacuate residents to the assembly point, take a headcount against the census, and remain with residents until the fire department releases the building.
After any fire or alarm activation, the Administrator documents the event, reports under SAF-02 and REC-02 if required, and notifies HHSC as required.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures the building meets Subchapter D, schedules inspections and drills, files forms 1127 and 1129 when required, and reviews drill results.
Performs and logs routine fire safety checks and coordinates vendor repairs.
Assesses and documents each resident's evacuation capability.
Attend orientation and drills and carry out evacuation procedures.

documentation: Sprinkler, alarm and extinguisher inspection and testing reports
Routine fire safety checklists
Fire drill records and corrective actions (kept at least 12 months)
Orientation attendance records covering emergency and evacuation procedures
Evacuation capability documentation in assessments
Copies of Forms 1127 and 1129 when sent
Posted evacuation plans

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, volunteers, residents and visitors
policies.purpose: To prevent and control the spread of infection among residents and staff through written procedures, standard precautions, employee exclusion and prompt reporting of reportable disease.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written infection prevention and control program as required by 26 TAC §553.261. It uses universal precautions for all residents. It complies with the state special waste rules and reports any resident with a reportable disease immediately to the local health authority and follows its direction. The program includes monitoring of key infectious agents and multidrug-resistant organisms, PPE and hand hygiene, routine cleaning and disinfecting of high-touch surfaces, daily removal of soiled items, safe linen handling, and a written rapid influenza diagnostic test procedure for residents with flu-like symptoms. Employees with a communicable disease are excluded from food handling or direct care for the period of communicability. TB screening and the vaccination policy for staff are handled under STF-04 and STF-05.

definitions.definition: Treating blood and body fluids of all residents as potentially infectious and using protective barriers accordingly.
A germ resistant to several antibiotics, such as MRSA or VRE.
A disease that state health rules require to be reported to the local health authority.
Personal protective equipment such as gloves, gowns, masks and eye protection.

procedures: The Administrator designates an infection control lead [NAME/ROLE] in writing. The lead is responsible for this program and its annual review.

The infection control lead maintains written procedures for monitoring key infectious agents and MDROs. Each month the lead reviews resident illness, infection and treatment information and logs it on [INFECTION SURVEILLANCE LOG].
All staff use universal precautions with every resident. Gloves, gowns, masks and eye protection are stocked in [LOCATIONS] and used based on the task and the risk.

Staff perform hand hygiene before and after resident contact, before handling food or medication, after glove removal, and after using the restroom. Handwashing supplies and alcohol-based hand rub are kept stocked.

Housekeeping staff clean and disinfect high-touch surfaces such as door knobs, handrails and light switches at least daily and whenever visibly soiled, using an EPA-registered disinfectant per label directions. Cleaning is logged on [CLEANING LOG].
Staff remove soiled items, such as soiled briefs, dressings and linens, from resident areas daily and sooner when needed, and dispose of them as directed in the procedure.

Staff handle, store, process and transport linens to prevent the spread of infection, as set out in DL-04: soiled linen is bagged at the point of use, carried away from the body, kept separate from clean linen, and washed under the facility's laundry procedure.

Sharps, blood-contaminated items and other special waste are placed in labeled puncture-resistant containers or bags and disposed of under the state special waste rules. The facility follows its bloodborne pathogen exposure control plan, including exposure follow-up.

If a resident has flu-like symptoms, the nurse or designated staff member notifies the physician, follows the written procedure for the rapid influenza diagnostic test, isolates or cohorts the resident as appropriate, and records the results and actions in the resident record.

When a resident has a reportable disease, the Administrator or nurse reports it to the local health authority immediately, documents the date, time and person contacted, and follows the authority's directions on isolation, testing, staff exclusion and visitors.

The Administrator excludes any employee who has a communicable disease that can be spread through food handling or direct care from those duties for the period of communicability. An employee with an infected wound or communicable disease may not work in food service. The exclusion and return date are recorded in the employee's file.
Staff must report their own symptoms of illness to the supervisor before the shift. The supervisor decides whether the employee works, is reassigned or is sent home.
The Administrator ensures that TB screening, the vaccination policy and exemptions are carried out and documented under STF-04 and STF-05, and keeps compliance records in personnel files.
The infection control lead trains staff on this policy at orientation and at least annually, and documents attendance.
The infection control lead reviews the program, surveillance data and outbreaks at least annually, and presents findings to the Administrator for quality assurance purposes (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Provides supplies, enforces employee exclusion, and makes reports to the local health authority.
Maintains procedures, surveillance log and training, and reviews the program annually.
Follow universal precautions, hand hygiene, cleaning and waste procedures.
Assesses ill residents, arranges testing and notifies the physician.

documentation: Written infection prevention and control procedures
Infection surveillance log
Cleaning logs
Records of reports to the local health authority
Rapid influenza test procedure and test results
Employee exclusion and return records
Training attendance records
TB screening and vaccination compliance records
Annual program review

policies.title: Smoking, Visitors and Pets
policies.applies_to: All staff, residents, representatives, visitors and volunteers
policies.purpose: To protect residents' right to visitors and communication, keep the environment safe from fire and other hazards, and set clear rules for smoking and animals that respect residents' rights.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] allows residents unrestricted communication and personal visitation with any person of their choice at any reasonable hour, including family and representatives of advocacy groups, and provides a private place for receiving visitors. HHSC and local authority employees are admitted as needed to serve a resident, and ombudsmen follow RR-03. Tobacco products may not be used in food preparation and service areas. Smoking elsewhere follows NFPA 101 and Subchapter D, and the facility's designated smoking areas are stated in the admission agreement. The facility may maintain an environment free of weapons and drugs. Pets and service animals that live in the facility are included in the emergency and evacuation plan.

definitions.definition: A time of day that does not unreasonably disrupt the resident's care or other residents' rest, as stated in the visitation guidelines. The resident's wishes are always considered.
A dog or other animal trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability.
The only place where smoking is permitted, selected to meet the fire code.

procedures: The Administrator posts the visitation guidelines in a common area. They state that residents may receive visitors of their choice at any reasonable hour and may communicate privately.
Staff greet visitors, ask them to sign in at [LOCATION] for safety and emergency headcount, and do not refuse a visitor the resident wants to see except under step 4.
The facility provides a private place, such as [ROOM/AREA], where each resident may meet visitors, and staff protect that privacy.

If a visitor appears to pose a risk (for example, is impaired, threatening or sick with a contagious illness), the staff member on duty calls the Administrator or the person in charge. Any restriction is limited to what is necessary for safety, is reviewed with the resident, and is documented. Restrictions based on a directive of HHSC or the local health authority are documented with the directive.
Staff immediately admit authorized HHSC and local authority employees who need access to serve a resident, and notify the Administrator. Ombudsman access is handled under RR-03.
Smoking and tobacco use is not permitted in food preparation or service areas at any time.

Smoking elsewhere is allowed only in designated smoking areas that comply with NFPA 101 and Subchapter D. The Administrator identifies the areas, posts signs, provides safe ashtrays or receptacles, and states the rules in the admission agreement (RR-04).
Residents who smoke are assessed for safe smoking during assessment and reassessment (ADM-02), and any supervision or safety needs are put in the service plan (ADM-03).
Staff check smoking areas and remove or empty smoking materials safely at least [FREQUENCY], and report any unsafe behavior to the Administrator.

The Administrator may maintain a weapon-free and drug-free environment. The admission agreement and posted notice state this, and staff handle any suspected violation under the Administrator's direction without violating resident rights.

Before a pet lives in the facility, the Administrator approves it in writing, confirms vaccinations, and notes who is responsible for its care. Service animals are admitted for residents who need them.
Any pet or service animal that lives in the facility is listed in the emergency and evacuation plan, and the EPC updates the plan whenever animals are added or removed (see SAF-05).
Visiting animals follow infection control rules (SAF-07), and animals are kept out of food preparation areas.
Staff report any complaint about a visitor, smoking or an animal to the Administrator, who handles it under RR-02.

responsibilities.duty: Posts the guidelines, approves any visitor restriction, designates smoking areas, approves pets and updates the emergency plan.
Welcome visitors, protect privacy, enforce smoking rules and report concerns.
Includes pets and service animals in the evacuation plan.

documentation: Posted visitation guidelines
Visitor log
Documentation of any visitor restriction and reason
Admission agreement provisions on smoking, weapons and drugs
Smoking safety assessments and service plan entries
Pet approval and vaccination records
Emergency plan section on animals

policies.title: Food Service and Therapeutic Diets
policies.applies_to: Dietary staff, the person responsible for food service, nursing and care staff, and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To provide residents nutritious, appetizing meals at regular times, to follow physician-ordered therapeutic diets, and to keep emergency food supplies.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] designates one person responsible for the total food service. It serves at least three meals or their equivalent daily at regular times, with no more than 16 hours between a substantial evening meal and breakfast unless HHSC approves an exception. Menus are planned one week ahead, are balanced and nutritious, are followed, and are kept as served for 30 days. Physician-ordered therapeutic diets are provided per the service plan, and diets that a layperson cannot customarily prepare are calculated by a qualified dietitian. The facility keeps at least a 4-day supply of staple foods and a 1-day supply of perishable foods on the premises. Staffing is sufficient to prepare and serve meals that meet each resident's nutritional and special dietary needs.

definitions.definition: A diet ordered by a physician for a medical condition, such as diabetic, low sodium or texture-modified.
A licensed or registered dietitian who calculates complex therapeutic diets.
Non-perishable foods such as canned goods, cereal and shelf-stable milk.

procedures: The Administrator designates in writing a person responsible for the total food service, [NAME/TITLE], and posts or records the designation in the dietary manual.

The food service manager schedules meals at regular times posted in the dining room. The facility serves at least three meals or their equivalent a day and plans so that no more than 16 hours pass between a substantial evening meal and breakfast. Any exception must first be approved by HHSC and the approval kept on file.
Each week the food service manager prepares menus for the following week, makes sure they are balanced and nutritious, and posts them where residents can see them.
Cooks follow the posted menu. When a substitution is made, the cook records the change on the menu the same day.
The food service manager keeps the menus as served, with variations recorded, for 30 days.

At admission and when diet orders change, the nurse or admissions staff records the resident's diet order, allergies, food preferences and swallowing or texture needs in the resident record and service plan, and gives the information to the kitchen the same day.
A therapeutic diet is served only on a physician's order. The kitchen keeps a current diet list and a diet-specific menu or substitution guide.

When a diet is one that a layperson cannot customarily prepare, the food service manager arranges for a qualified dietitian to calculate it, and keeps the dietitian's calculation or diet plan on file.

Staff serve each resident the right diet. Before serving, a second staff member checks the diet list against the tray or plate for residents on therapeutic diets, and offers alternatives within the order when a resident refuses a meal.
Care staff monitor and record significant changes in intake, weight loss or swallowing difficulty, and report them to the nurse, who follows HCS-05.

The food service manager keeps at least a 4-day supply of staple foods and a 1-day supply of perishable foods on the premises based on the current census. The food service manager checks the supply monthly and logs it on [FOOD SUPPLY LOG].

The Administrator checks the staffing pattern at least monthly to make sure there are enough staff to prepare and serve meals that meet residents' nutritional and special dietary needs, and adjusts the schedule when the census or diet needs change.
Food service staff handle food under DL-02.
The Administrator reviews resident dining feedback and complaints at least quarterly, takes corrective action, and records the review for quality assurance (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Designates the food service manager, ensures staffing and supplies, and obtains any HHSC meal-interval approval.
Plans and posts menus, ensures diets are followed, keeps menus and supplies, and arranges for a dietitian when needed.
Documents diet orders, monitors intake and weight, and communicates with the physician.
Prepare and serve the correct diet and record menu variations.

documentation: Written designation of person responsible for food service
Posted meal times
Weekly menus as served for 30 days, with variations
Physician diet orders
Dietitian calculations for complex diets
Current diet list
Food supply log
HHSC approval for any meal-interval exception
Resident dining feedback review

policies.title: Food Safety and Sanitation
policies.applies_to: All dietary staff, other employees who handle food, and the person responsible for food service
policies.purpose: To prevent foodborne illness by controlling food temperatures, sources, storage, employee hygiene and sanitation.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] stores, prepares and serves food safely. Potentially hazardous foods are held at 45°F or below, and hot food is held at 140°F or above. Reheated food reaches 165°F. Refrigerators are kept at 41°F or below and freezers at 0°F or below, with a thermometer in the warmest area of each. Food comes from sources that comply with food laws. Food removed from its original container is sealed, labeled, and dated if perishable. Employees use effective hair restraints and wash hands after using the lavatory, dishes are washed sanitarily, and surfaces are cleaned, rinsed and sanitized. No tobacco is used in food areas. A facility housing 17 or more residents also complies with the state retail food rules and local health ordinances.

definitions.definition: Food that requires temperature control to prevent the growth of harmful bacteria, such as meat, dairy and cooked rice.
To reduce germs on a cleaned surface to a safe level, using heat or an approved chemical at the correct concentration.
The temperature range between cold-holding and hot-holding limits in which bacteria multiply quickly.

procedures: The food service manager buys food only from sources that comply with food laws, and keeps receipts or invoices. Home-canned or unapproved foods are not served.
At delivery, staff check that food is in good condition and that cold items are cold. They reject damaged or temperature-abused items and put away perishables immediately.

Staff keep refrigerators at 41°F or below and freezers at 0°F or below. A thermometer is kept in the warmest area of each unit. A designated cook reads and records the temperatures on [TEMPERATURE LOG] at least daily, and reports any out-of-range reading to the food service manager, who corrects it and decides whether food must be discarded.

Potentially hazardous foods are held at 45°F or below when cold. Hot food is held at 140°F or above during service. Cooks check with a calibrated food thermometer and record temperatures for each meal on [FOOD TEMPERATURE LOG].
Staff reheat leftover or previously cooked food to 165°F before serving. Food that falls in the danger zone for longer than allowed by the facility's time guide is discarded.
Food removed from its original container is stored in a sealed, covered container, labeled with the contents, and dated if perishable. Staff discard food past its use-by date.
Food and supplies are stored off the floor in clean, dry, pest-free areas. Chemicals and cleaning supplies are stored separately from food.

Employees wear effective hair restraints while preparing or serving food, keep clothing and fingernails clean, and wash hands before starting work, after using the lavatory, after handling raw foods, after touching the face or hair, and as often as needed. Handwashing sinks are kept stocked with soap and paper towels.

Dishes, utensils and equipment are washed, rinsed and sanitized by the dish machine or three-compartment sink method. Staff test and record sanitizer concentration on [SANITIZER LOG] each shift. Dishes are air-dried and stored protected.
Food contact surfaces and equipment are cleaned, rinsed and sanitized after each use. The food service manager keeps a daily and weekly cleaning schedule and initials it.
No tobacco is used in food preparation or service areas.
An employee with a communicable disease or an infected wound may not work in food service. The food service manager sends the employee home or reassigns the employee and follows SAF-07 for return.
The food service manager trains all food handlers on this policy at hire and at least annually and documents it.

If the facility houses 17 or more residents, the Administrator confirms compliance with the state retail food rules and local health ordinances, keeps any required permit or inspection reports, and corrects any findings promptly.
The food service manager or Administrator inspects the kitchen monthly with [KITCHEN SANITATION CHECKLIST], records findings and corrective action, and reports results for quality assurance (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Supervises safe food handling, ensures temperature and sanitizer logs are kept, trains staff and inspects the kitchen monthly.
Follow hygiene, temperature, labeling and sanitation procedures and report problems.
Provides equipment and supplies, ensures compliance with retail food rules if applicable, and reviews inspection results.

documentation: Refrigerator and freezer temperature logs
Food temperature logs
Sanitizer concentration logs
Cleaning schedules
Monthly kitchen inspection checklist
Food handler training records
Invoices from food sources
Retail food permits or inspection reports, if applicable

policies.title: Activities and Social Programming
policies.applies_to: All residents, including STAR+PLUS HCBS members; activity staff, attendants and the manager
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident has regular, meaningful opportunities for social, recreational, religious and community participation that fit the resident's preferences and abilities, and to meet the Texas HHSC activity-program requirement and the STAR+PLUS weekly social-activity requirement.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides an activity or social program for residents at least weekly, as required by 26 TAC §553.261(d). Programming is built from each resident's assessed interests, involvement patterns and abilities. For residents who receive STAR+PLUS HCBS assisted living services, [AGENCY NAME] offers at least four social activities per week (STAR+PLUS Handbook §§7250–7252). Residents may take part in social, religious and community groups and may practice their chosen religion (26 TAC §553.267(a)(3)(B),(C)). Participation is always voluntary. No resident is required to attend, and no resident is penalized for declining.

definitions.definition: A planned schedule of social, recreational, spiritual, physical, creative and community activities offered to residents.
A resident who receives Medicaid assisted living services through a managed care organization (MCO) contracted with [AGENCY NAME].
The staff member designated by the manager to plan, schedule, lead and document activities.

procedures: The Manager designates an Activity Coordinator in writing and names a backup who covers absences so that programming is never skipped.

At admission, the Activity Coordinator or Manager interviews the resident and family or representative about life history, hobbies, faith practices, preferred times of day, cultural and language preferences, and activities the resident dislikes.

The Activity Coordinator records the resident's involvement patterns and preferred activities in the resident's comprehensive assessment and Individual Service Plan (ISP) (see ADM-02 and ADM-03), and updates them at each reassessment and on significant change.

By the 25th of each month, the Activity Coordinator prepares the next month's calendar. It lists at least four social activities per week and includes a mix of group, small-group and one-to-one options, physical activity, cognitive activity, creative activity, spiritual activity and community outings.

The Manager reviews and approves the calendar. The approved calendar is posted in a common area, given to residents and representatives, and read aloud or offered in large print or the resident's primary language on request (see RR-08).
Scheduled activities are offered at varied times, including some mornings, afternoons and evenings, so that residents with different routines and night-shift sleep patterns can take part.

Staff invite each resident personally. Staff provide the mobility, vision, hearing and cueing support residents need to take part, and provide in-room or one-to-one activity for residents who cannot or prefer not to join group events.

Residents who wish to attend religious services, or to join community, civic or social groups, are supported. The facility helps arrange transportation under DL-05 when it is available, helps residents contact clergy or visitors, and respects the resident's choice not to participate.

For residents with Alzheimer's disease or related disorders, the Activity Coordinator adapts activities to the resident's abilities and uses person-centered approaches taught in dementia training (see HCS-06 and STF-03).

Staff who lead activities follow fall-prevention, infection-control and safety practices, including inspecting equipment and space, and keeping smoking and open-flame items out of activities (see HCS-07, SAF-07 and SAF-08).
The Activity Coordinator completes an attendance sheet for every activity. It records the date, activity, leader, residents attending, and whether each resident is a STAR+PLUS member.

Each month, the Manager compares the attendance sheets with the calendar and confirms that at least one activity occurred each week and that at least four social activities occurred each week for STAR+PLUS members. If a week falls short, the Manager documents the reason and adds make-up activities.

The Activity Coordinator documents in the resident record, at least quarterly, each resident's participation level, any refusals or declining interest, and changes in mood or withdrawal. Significant changes are reported to the Manager, who follows HCS-05 where indicated.

The Activity Coordinator collects resident feedback at least quarterly through a resident council, surveys or individual conversations. The Manager considers it in planning and in the QA review under GOV-04.
The Manager keeps calendars and attendance records for review by HHSC surveyors and MCO service coordinators, and makes them available to the MCO on request.

responsibilities.duty: Designates the Activity Coordinator and backup, approves monthly calendars, verifies weekly and STAR+PLUS minimums are met, and reviews resident feedback.
Interviews residents about preferences, plans and leads activities, keeps attendance records, and documents participation.
Invite and assist residents to take part, support in-room activities, and report changes in mood or participation.
May suggest activities, choose whether to take part, and give feedback.

documentation: Monthly activity calendars
Activity attendance sheets showing STAR+PLUS members
Activity preferences in the comprehensive assessment and ISP
Quarterly participation notes
Resident council minutes or survey results
Documentation of make-up activities and reasons for any missed week

policies.title: Housekeeping, Laundry and Maintenance
policies.applies_to: Housekeeping, laundry, maintenance and direct-care staff; the manager; contracted maintenance vendors
policies.purpose: To provide residents with a clean, safe, sanitary and decent living environment, to prevent infection through proper cleaning and linen handling, and to keep the building and its fire protection systems in good repair.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a safe and decent living environment for every resident (26 TAC §553.267(a)(3)(F)). Staffing is sufficient to maintain order, safety and cleanliness and to assist with laundry (26 TAC §553.253(c)(3)(A),(D)). Staff clean and disinfect environmental surfaces, remove soiled items from the environment at least daily, and handle linens in a way that prevents infection (26 TAC §553.261(f)(5),(7)). The building and its fire protection systems are maintained to the standards of 26 TAC Subchapter D that apply to this facility's type and size.

definitions.definition: Removal of visible soil and debris from surfaces using detergent and water.
Use of an EPA-registered disinfectant, applied according to label directions including contact time, to reduce germs on surfaces.
Surfaces frequently touched by residents and staff, such as door handles, handrails, light switches, call devices, remote controls and bathroom fixtures.
Any linen, clothing, brief, dressing, trash or other item contaminated with body fluids or waste.

procedures: The Manager assigns housekeeping, laundry and maintenance duties in writing, with a daily and weekly schedule for each area, including resident rooms, bathrooms, common areas, kitchen, dining area, laundry and entrances.

Housekeeping staff use only EPA-registered disinfectants approved by the Manager. They follow label directions for dilution and contact time and keep safety data sheets available. Chemicals are stored locked and out of resident reach, especially in dementia-care areas.

Staff clean and disinfect high-touch surfaces at least daily. They clean bathrooms and shared equipment between uses, and disinfect rooms of residents with suspected or confirmed infection according to SAF-07.

Staff remove soiled items, trash and used personal-care supplies from resident rooms and common areas at least daily, and immediately when contaminated. Staff wear gloves and other personal protective equipment as required in SAF-07 and perform hand hygiene after removing it.

Soiled linen and clothing are handled with minimal agitation, bagged at the point of use, and kept separate from clean linen. Soiled linen is never placed on the floor, in food areas or on clean surfaces.

Laundry is done on a schedule that provides residents clean clothing and bed linen. Bed linen is changed at least weekly and whenever soiled. Staff assist residents who need help with personal laundry. Clean linen is dried completely, stored covered and off the floor, and transported separately from soiled linen.
Staff label resident clothing, and handle residents' personal items with respect. Staff report lost or damaged items to the Manager, who follows RR-05.

The Manager provides enough housekeeping and laundry coverage, using dedicated staff or scheduled attendant time, so that attendants are not pulled from resident supervision or safety duties. The staffing pattern is reviewed under STF-01.

The Maintenance Designee inspects the building at least weekly for hazards. These include slippery floors, loose rugs, broken furniture, burned-out lighting, damaged handrails, blocked exits, water leaks, pests, unsafe water temperatures and inoperable call devices. Findings are written on a maintenance log.

Residents and staff report repair needs to the Manager or Maintenance Designee at once. Hazards are removed or made safe the same day, and repairs are completed according to a written priority list: immediate safety, then resident comfort, then cosmetic.

The Maintenance Designee maintains the fire protection systems as required by 26 TAC Subchapter D for this facility. They keep the sprinkler system (if required), the manual fire alarm and smoke detection, fire extinguishers and emergency lighting in working order. They arrange for testing and inspection by qualified contractors and keep the reports (see SAF-06).
The facility keeps heating and cooling systems working so that indoor temperatures are comfortable and safe for residents, and arranges service promptly when a system fails (see SAF-05).
The facility maintains pest control by a licensed pest-control provider and keeps service records. Kitchen waste is removed and stored according to DL-02.
The Manager inspects housekeeping and maintenance at least monthly using a checklist. Deficiencies are corrected promptly, and trends are reviewed in the QA process (see GOV-04).

Housekeeping and laundry staff complete orientation and annual training on infection control, chemical safety, resident rights and privacy, and reporting of abuse, neglect and exploitation (see STF-03). Staff who have recurring resident contact complete the required Alzheimer's/dementia training.

responsibilities.duty: Assigns duties and schedules, ensures staffing is sufficient for cleanliness and laundry, performs monthly inspections, and approves repairs and vendors.
Clean, disinfect and remove soiled items on schedule, and handle linen to prevent infection.
Performs weekly hazard inspections, completes repairs, and maintains fire protection systems and records.
Keep resident areas orderly and safe, assist with personal laundry, and report hazards immediately.

documentation: Housekeeping and laundry schedules and cleaning checklists
Weekly maintenance and hazard inspection logs
Repair requests and completion records
Fire protection system inspection, test and maintenance reports
Pest-control service records
Monthly environmental inspection checklists
Training records for housekeeping, laundry and maintenance staff

policies.title: Transportation (Non-Emergency and Evacuation)
policies.applies_to: Staff and volunteers who drive or accompany residents; the manager; the emergency preparedness coordinator
policies.purpose: To provide for the safe, disclosed and consistent transportation of residents for routine needs and during an evacuation, and to coordinate evacuation transportation with the facility's emergency plan.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] discloses any facility-provided transportation, and any charge for it, in the written admission agreement and rate schedule before admission (26 TAC §553.259(a)(2)). Non-emergency transportation is provided according to this policy. Transportation for evacuation is one of the eight core functions of the emergency plan required by 26 TAC §553.275. The plan includes the procedure for safely transporting residents, and for notifying drivers, and the employer of any non-facility driver, of the evacuation. Sufficient trained staff accompany evacuating residents and remain with them. Residents may leave the facility temporarily or permanently, subject to any contractual or financial obligations.

definitions.definition: Scheduled or routine travel such as medical appointments, outings, religious services and shopping.
Movement of residents to a receiving facility or shelter during an emergency, according to the emergency plan.
A driver who is not employed by [AGENCY NAME], such as a contracted bus or ambulance company.

procedures: Before admission, the Manager states in the admission agreement and rate schedule whether the facility provides transportation, to what destinations and on what days, the charge (if any) and the notice required to schedule a ride. The Manager explains this to the resident and representative (see RR-04 and ADM-01).
Residents and representatives request rides at least [NUMBER] business days ahead where possible. Staff record the request, destination, time, assistance needed and who will accompany the resident.

The Manager confirms that each facility driver holds a valid Texas driver license, completed the facility's orientation, and has a clear driving record check. A copy of the license is kept in the personnel file (see STF-06). Drivers who are not the resident's attendant do not leave the building short of required supervision (see STF-01).
Before each trip, staff inspect the vehicle for working seat belts, wheelchair securements, lights, tires, fuel and a first-aid kit. They record the inspection.

Staff identify the resident's mobility, medication, behavioral and toileting needs before the trip. They send needed medications, medical orders, the face sheet, emergency contacts and any advance directive information with the resident or the escort, as the resident's needs require (see RR-06 and HCS-02).
Residents are seated with seat belts fastened, and wheelchairs are secured with approved tie-downs. Residents are never left unattended in a vehicle.
For residents with dementia or elopement risk, staff are assigned to escort and stay with them throughout the trip. Staff follow SAF-03 if a resident goes missing.

If an accident, injury, illness or behavioral incident occurs during a trip, staff call 911 when needed and notify the Manager and the resident's representative immediately. They document the event under SAF-02 and report it to HHSC and others where required (see REC-02).

A resident who chooses to leave the facility temporarily or permanently with family or another party is allowed to do so, subject to contractual or financial obligations. Staff record the departure and expected return time, give any medications ordered for the absence per HCS-03, and note the return in the record.

The Emergency Preparedness Coordinator includes in the emergency plan the procedures for safely transporting residents. This covers vehicles available, wheelchair and stretcher needs, seating and loading order, medications and supplies to travel with residents, and the destination (see SAF-05).

If the facility relies on a non-facility driver or transport company, the Emergency Preparedness Coordinator keeps written arrangements with that provider. The facility notifies the driver, and the driver's employer, of the evacuation when the facility decides to evacuate, and keeps a record of the notification.

When an evacuation is ordered, the Manager or designee assigns enough trained staff to accompany evacuating residents and remain with them at the receiving location. A resident roster, medications and records travel with the staff.

Staff account for each resident by roster at loading, on arrival and at return, and the Manager records the times. The facility notifies the HHSC regional office and the local Emergency Management Coordinator of the decision to evacuate, as required under SAF-05.

The Manager reviews transportation arrangements, vehicle checks and evacuation transport procedures at least annually. The review is repeated within 30 days after any event, drill shortcoming or rule change, and the plan is updated (see GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Discloses transportation terms, approves drivers and vehicles, assigns escorts and reviews trip and incident records.
Maintains the evacuation transportation provisions in the emergency plan, including arrangements with non-facility drivers and notification of them.
Inspect vehicles, secure and supervise residents, carry needed records and medications, and report incidents.
Request rides in advance and share information on special needs.

documentation: Admission agreement and rate schedule showing transportation terms and charges
Trip request and transportation logs
Vehicle inspection records and driver license copies
Incident reports from trips
Resident departure and return records
Evacuation transportation section of the emergency plan, written arrangements with outside transport providers, and notification records
Evacuation rosters and drill records

policies.title: Staffing Levels and Supervision
policies.applies_to: All direct-care and support staff, the manager and backup manager; Type A and Type B facilities
policies.purpose: To make sure the facility always has enough qualified staff on duty, based on residents' assessed needs, to provide care, supervision, safety and evacuation, and to meet Texas HHSC staffing, disclosure and posting requirements.
policies.policy: Chapter 553 does not set a numeric staff-to-resident ratio. [AGENCY NAME] sets staffing ratios based on residents' needs as identified in their service plans (26 TAC §553.253(c)(1)). An attendant is in the facility at all times when residents are in the facility. Attendants may also perform other functions the facility requires (26 TAC §553.253(b)). Staff are sufficient to maintain order, safety and cleanliness, assist with medications, prepare meals, assist with laundry, supervise residents and ensure safe evacuation. Night staffing depends on facility type and size (26 TAC §§553.5, 553.3, 553.253). A small facility is licensed for 16 or fewer residents, and a large facility for 17 or more. At night, staff in a small Type A facility are immediately available. In a large Type A facility and in any Type B facility, staff are immediately available and awake. The normal 24-hour staffing pattern is disclosed to prospective residents and families before admission and is posted monthly (26 TAC §§553.253(c)(2), 553.271). Employees are paid at least the federal minimum wage under 29 USC 206 and any higher rate required by law or set by the facility.

definitions.definition: A staff member who provides direct care and supervision to residents and who may also perform other functions the facility requires.
Staff are on the premises and able to respond to a resident without delay. In a small Type A facility they need not be awake.
Staff on duty are alert and not sleeping. This applies at night in large Type A and all Type B facilities.
The written schedule of the number and type of staff on duty on each shift in a typical 24-hour period.
Small means licensed for 16 or fewer residents. Large means 17 or more.
Type A: residents can evacuate without staff help and need no routine night attendance. Type B: residents may need help to evacuate and need night attendance, but may not be permanently bedfast.

procedures: The Manager determines the facility's type (A or B) and size (small or large) from the license and records it at the top of the staffing plan. The night-staffing standard that applies is recorded on the same page.

The Manager reviews every resident's service plan and assessment (see ADM-02 and ADM-03). From these, the Manager identifies the care, supervision, medication, behavior, evacuation and mealtime needs of the resident group on each shift.

The Manager sets staffing ratios and numbers per shift in writing from those needs. This covers personal care, medication administration by authorized staff, meal preparation and service, laundry, housekeeping, supervision and safe evacuation. The Manager records the reasoning used and the date.

An attendant is scheduled so that one is in the facility at all times that any resident is present. The Manager never schedules a gap in coverage, including during breaks, shift changes and when the sole attendant calls out.

Night shifts are staffed to the facility's standard. A small Type A facility has staff immediately available. A large Type A facility, and every Type B facility regardless of size, has staff immediately available and awake. The Manager checks night staff by unannounced visits or other spot checks at least monthly and documents them.

The Manager confirms that on every shift enough staff on duty are authorized to administer medications under HCS-02 (a licensed nurse, a permitted medication aide, or an RN-delegated employee) whenever residents need medication administration.

The Manager schedules enough staff on each shift to evacuate residents safely, based on the residents' evacuation capability. The Manager reviews this after fire drills and at each reassessment (see SAF-06).
The Manager prepares a written normal 24-hour staffing pattern showing the number and type of staff per shift. It is reviewed at least monthly and any time resident needs change significantly.
Before admission, the Manager gives the normal 24-hour staffing pattern to every prospective resident and family or representative and documents that they received it (see ADM-01).
The Manager posts the current staffing pattern in a public area each month, with the other required postings, and records the date of each posting (see GOV-06).

The Manager keeps the daily staff schedule, time records and sign-in sheets, and compares actual staffing to the posted pattern at least weekly. Variances and the reasons for them, such as call-outs, are documented along with the corrective action taken.
The Manager keeps an on-call list and a procedure for filling absences, including part-time and agency staff who have met STF-02 and STF-03 requirements before working alone with residents.

Staff who are new to the facility are scheduled alongside experienced staff during their first-16-hour on-the-job training period, as described in STF-03. They are not counted as the sole attendant until orientation and competency requirements are met.

Full-time attendants must be at least 18 years of age or a high school graduate. Staff younger than 18 who are not full-time attendants are never left as the only person responsible for residents. The Manager verifies age or diploma and keeps the proof in the personnel file (see STF-06).

If staffing falls below the facility's standard, the Manager takes immediate steps, such as calling in on-call staff, working a shift personally or [BACKUP MANAGER NAME] doing so, and, if needed, pauses admissions and adjusts services. The Manager documents the event and the resolution.

The Manager verifies that all employees are paid at least the federal minimum wage under 29 USC 206 and any higher rate required by law. Payroll records are reviewed against time records at each pay period.

At least quarterly, the Manager reviews incidents, falls, complaints and resident acuity changes to decide whether staffing ratios need to be increased. Results are documented and reported in QA review (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Sets staffing ratios from service plans, ensures attendant coverage and the correct night standard, prepares and posts the staffing pattern, and monitors actual staffing.
Covers the Manager's duties when the Manager is absent.
Remain on duty and supervise residents, never leave residents unattended, and report staffing shortfalls at once.
Provides the budget and resources needed to meet staffing standards and wage laws.

documentation: Written staffing plan showing facility type and size and ratio rationale
Normal 24-hour staffing pattern, with posting dates
Proof of disclosure to prospective residents
Daily schedules, sign-in sheets and time records
Night-shift spot-check records
Variance and call-out reports
Proof of age or diploma for attendants
Payroll records
Quarterly staffing review

policies.title: Background Checks and Employee Registries
policies.applies_to: All applicants, employees and contractors with direct resident contact or access; the manager
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] does not hire or retain anyone who is barred from working with residents, and to comply with the criminal history and registry requirements of Texas Health and Safety Code Chapter 250 and 26 TAC §553.257.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] complies with Texas Health and Safety Code Chapter 250. Before hire, the Manager searches the Employee Misconduct Registry (EMR) and the HHSC Nurse Aide Registry (NAR). [AGENCY NAME] does not hire or retain anyone listed as unemployable or convicted of an offense that bars employment under HSC §250.006 (26 TAC §553.257). EMR and NAR searches are repeated at least every 12 months. An applicant who lived in another state in the past five years must have a name-based criminal history check in each of those states. The person may be hired pending results but may not work in a direct-contact position until the results are received and cleared. [AGENCY NAME] suspends, and does not reinstate until appeals are exhausted, any employee HHSC finds has engaged in reportable conduct.

definitions.definition: The Employee Misconduct Registry maintained by HHSC, listing unlicensed persons found to have committed reportable conduct.
The Nurse Aide Registry maintained by HHSC.
A conviction listed in HSC §250.006 that bars a person from employment in a direct-contact position.
A position in which the employee has face-to-face contact with residents or access to their living areas or records.
Abuse or neglect that causes or may cause harm, sexual abuse, financial exploitation of $25 or more, and emotional or verbal abuse that causes harm.

procedures: The employment application asks about criminal convictions, EMR or NAR listings, and every state of residence in the past five years. The Manager reviews it before any offer is made.

Before the employee's first day, the Manager searches the EMR and NAR for the applicant, and prints or saves the results with the date and the name of the person who searched. Anyone listed as unemployable is not hired.

The Manager requests the criminal history check required by Chapter 250 for the applicant and documents that the request was submitted and the date and result received. Results are reviewed only by the Manager or [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] and kept confidential.

If a conviction on the §250.006 list appears, or the applicant is listed as unemployable on a registry, the applicant is not hired and the offer is withdrawn. If a current employee is found to be barred, the employee is removed from direct contact at once and employment is ended. The Manager documents the decision.
The applicant signs a disclosure statement before hire stating whether he or she has any conviction listed in HSC §250.006 and listing every state of residence in the past five years.
For each state of residence in the past five years other than Texas, the Manager obtains a name-based criminal history check from that state, and files the results.

An applicant may be hired while out-of-state results are pending, but only in a position without direct resident contact. The Manager puts a written restriction in the personnel file. The restriction is lifted in writing only after all results are received and cleared.
The employee receives and signs the required EMR notification and acknowledgment, and the facility keeps a copy.
The employee signs a statement acknowledging criminal liability for failure to report abuse, neglect and exploitation, and understands the duty to report to HHSC at 1-800-458-9858 (see SAF-01).

The Manager sets a tickler for each employee's annual registry search and repeats the EMR and NAR searches at least every 12 months. Results are filed in the personnel file. A new listing leads to immediate removal from direct contact and the termination actions above.
Contractors and volunteers who have unsupervised resident contact or work in resident areas go through the same checks before they begin work, and are not left alone with residents until cleared.

If HHSC notifies [AGENCY NAME] that an employee is found to have engaged in reportable conduct, the Manager suspends the employee from duty immediately. The employee is not reinstated until all appeals are exhausted and the finding is no longer in effect.
When the Manager learns of reportable conduct, the Manager reports it to HHSC at 1-800-458-9858 and follows SAF-01 and REC-02. The Manager keeps the report and any outcome in a confidential file.

The Manager does a quarterly audit of personnel files to verify that every file contains the criminal history documentation, EMR and NAR results with dates within the last 12 months, the signed disclosure statement, the signed criminal-liability statement and any out-of-state checks. Gaps are corrected within 5 business days.
Criminal history information and registry results are kept confidential, stored in locked or access-controlled files, and used only for employment decisions.

Reviews barring-offense decisions and ensures resources are available for checks.
Give complete and truthful information, sign the required statements, and report new convictions or registry actions immediately.

policies.title: Hiring, Orientation and Ongoing Training
policies.applies_to: All employees, including the manager, attendants, nurses, medication aides, housekeeping, kitchen and maintenance staff
policies.purpose: To make sure every staff member is qualified, oriented and trained before taking on responsibilities and stays competent, as required by Texas HHSC rules for assisted living facilities, including Alzheimer's and dementia training and medication aide requirements.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] documents that each staff member is competent to provide the personal care required before he or she assumes responsibilities (26 TAC §553.253(d)). Every employee completes a 4-hour orientation before taking on any job responsibilities. Attendants complete 16 hours of on-the-job supervision and training within their first 16 hours of employment after orientation. Direct-care staff complete 6 documented hours of training each year, including 1 hour on fall prevention and 1 hour on behavior management. Nurses, CNAs and medication aides complete an annual geriatric in-service. All staff receive Alzheimer's disease and related-disorder training in line with 26 TAC §553.254, and the facility keeps a policy for all staff on residents with Alzheimer's disease or related disorders (26 TAC §553.255). Medication administration is limited to the people authorized under HCS-02, consistent with HHSC Provider Letter 2023-22.

definitions.definition: The 4-hour introductory training every employee completes before taking on any job responsibilities.
Supervised training for attendants, 16 hours, in the first 16 hours of work after orientation.
A documented check, by observation or test, that a person can perform a task or apply a training topic correctly.
Employees who provide personal care or hands-on care to residents.
A person holding a Texas medication aide permit who may administer medications under the supervision of a nurse on duty or on call.

procedures: The Manager interviews each applicant, verifies education, licenses, certifications and references, and confirms completion of the checks in STF-02 and the health screening in STF-04 before the first day of work.
The Manager gives each new employee a written job description and the facility's policies, and the employee signs that they were received.

Before the employee has any job responsibilities, the Manager or a designee provides a 4-hour orientation. It covers reporting of abuse and neglect, confidentiality, universal precautions, conditions that must be reported to the Manager, resident rights, and emergency and evacuation procedures. Date, hours, trainer and topics are recorded and the employee signs.

Attendants then complete 16 hours of supervised on-the-job training within their first 16 hours of employment after orientation. Topics include assistance with activities of daily living, common health conditions, accident prevention, emergency first aid (Heimlich maneuver, falls, lacerations, sudden changes in condition), disruptive behavior, behavior management and fall prevention.

A trained, experienced staff member supervises the OJT. The Manager documents each skill demonstrated and that competency was observed, and signs off when complete. The employee does not work alone with residents until then.

Before performing personal care, personal care staff complete 4 hours of Alzheimer's disease and related-disorder training with a competency evaluation, as required by 26 TAC §553.254. Each year thereafter they complete 2 hours of continuing education on this subject.
The Manager completes 4 hours of Alzheimer's/dementia training with a competency evaluation, then 2 hours of annual continuing education on the subject.

Non-direct staff with recurring resident contact, such as housekeeping, front desk and maintenance, complete training and a competency evaluation on Alzheimer's disease, person-centered care and behaviors.

Dementia-related training from a previous employer carries over if the gap in employment is less than 2 years and the certificate is on file. The Manager issues certificates to staff and keeps copies in the personnel file under STF-06.

All staff are given the facility's policy on staff and residents with Alzheimer's disease and related disorders (HCS-06), and sign that they have read it. The §553.254 training satisfies the training content of that policy where applicable.

Direct-care staff complete 6 documented hours of in-service education each year by their hire-date anniversary. The 6 hours must include 1 hour on fall prevention and 1 hour on behavior management. Education is competency-based, with a quiz, demonstration or observation.
Nurses, CNAs and medication aides complete an annual geriatric in-service. The topics are chosen from the list in 26 TAC §553.253(d)(4), and the Manager tracks due dates.

The Manager verifies medication aide permits before the employee administers any medication. The Manager records the permit number and expiration date and confirms the employee works under a nurse on duty or on call, per HCS-02. Permits are renewed annually, and after the first renewal 7 hours of continuing education are required for renewal. The Manager tracks this and removes the employee from medication duties immediately if the permit lapses.
Staff who do tasks delegated by an RN complete the delegation training and have a documented RN delegation under HCS-04 before performing them.

The Manager completes the 24-hour assisted living management course by the first anniversary of appointment, with 8 hours on the standards completed within 3 months, and 12 hours of continuing education each year.

The Manager keeps a training matrix with every employee's hire date, orientation, OJT, dementia training, annual in-service hours, permits and renewal dates, and reviews it monthly. Overdue items are scheduled within 14 days, and the employee does not perform tasks he or she is not trained for.
The Manager evaluates each employee's performance and competency at 90 days and then annually, and retrains anyone found lacking in a skill. The Manager documents the retraining.

responsibilities.duty: Conducts or arranges orientation and OJT, tracks all training and permit dates, verifies competency, completes own required courses, and keeps training records.
Supervise OJT, demonstrate skills and attest to competency.
Provide medication and delegation training and complete the required geriatric in-service.
Complete required training on time, keep permits current and perform only tasks for which they are trained and authorized.

policies.title: Employee Health and TB Screening
policies.applies_to: All employees, including managers, attendants, medication aides, nurses, dietary, housekeeping and maintenance staff. Outside-resource contractors with resident contact are covered under the contractor provisions.
policies.purpose: To protect residents and staff from communicable disease by screening employees for tuberculosis (TB), excluding ill employees when required, and documenting compliance for HHSC review.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] screens every employee for TB within 2 weeks of the start of employment and annually after that, following CDC guidelines (26 TAC §553.261). The facility maintains written communicable disease policies for employees and residents, including TB screening. An employee with a communicable disease that can be transmitted through food handling or direct care is excluded from those duties for the period of communicability. Outside-resource contractors must provide evidence of TB screening on request. Initial TB screening documentation is kept in the personnel file (26 TAC §553.257). The facility keeps evidence of compliance with local and state health codes on employee and resident health status.

definitions.definition: A CDC-consistent process that may include a symptom review and a TB test (skin test or blood test), with follow-up medical evaluation for a positive result or symptoms, as directed by the facility's consulting physician or registered nurse.
The time during which an infected person can transmit a disease to others, as determined by a physician or the local health authority.
A person or agency (for example, a home health or hospice provider, therapist or private-duty caregiver) that provides services to residents under arrangement with the facility or the resident.
Hands-on personal care, medication assistance or other services provided directly to a resident.

procedures: The Administrator designates the Infection Prevention Coordinator, who administers this policy, and keeps the TB screening protocol approved by the facility's consulting physician or registered nurse in the Infection Control Manual.
At the job offer, the Administrator or designee informs the candidate in writing of the TB screening requirement and the 2-week deadline, and gives the candidate the health screening form.

On or before the first day of work, HR collects any prior TB screening results the candidate has and checks whether they meet the facility's protocol and CDC guidelines. Acceptable prior results are filed. Otherwise screening is scheduled.
The employee completes initial TB screening no later than 14 calendar days after the start date. HR records the due date on the Personnel Compliance Tracker on the first day of work.
If initial screening is not completed by day 14, the Administrator removes the employee from the schedule until documentation is received and records the removal on the tracker.

A positive test or TB symptoms are referred promptly to a physician or the local health department. The employee does not provide direct care or food service until a physician or the health authority gives written clearance, which is kept in a confidential medical section of the personnel file.
HR files the initial TB screening documentation in the personnel file (26 TAC §553.257) and keeps detailed medical information in a separate, confidential section.

Each year, no later than the anniversary month of the employee's last screening, the Infection Prevention Coordinator schedules annual TB screening in the manner the facility's protocol requires under CDC guidelines. HR documents the completion date and result.

Employees must report to their supervisor before their next shift if they have symptoms of a communicable disease, such as fever with cough, vomiting or diarrhea, an infectious rash, or a diagnosed communicable disease. Supervisors do not penalize employees for reporting.

The supervisor and Infection Prevention Coordinator decide whether the employee is excluded from direct care or food handling. The employee is excluded for the period of communicability and returns only after a physician's or health authority's clearance, or after the symptom-free interval the facility's protocol specifies.
The Infection Prevention Coordinator records each exclusion (employee, dates, reason category and return date) in the Employee Illness Log. The log excludes unnecessary diagnostic detail.

Employees with potential exposure to blood or body fluids follow the facility's bloodborne pathogen exposure control plan under 29 CFR 1910.1030, including hepatitis B vaccine offers, immediate first aid and post-exposure medical evaluation.

Before an outside-resource contractor begins work with residents, and at least annually, the Infection Prevention Coordinator requests written evidence of the contractor's TB screening and files it in the contractor file. The facility provides the evidence to HHSC on request.

The Administrator keeps current evidence of compliance with local and state health codes on employee and resident health status, and the Infection Prevention Coordinator reports any disease required to be reported to the local health authority (see REC-02).

Monthly, HR reviews the Personnel Compliance Tracker for TB screenings due within 60 days and sends written reminders. The Administrator reviews overdue items and reports results to the QA Committee quarterly.

responsibilities.duty: Enforces the TB screening deadlines, removes noncompliant employees from the schedule, and ensures health code compliance evidence is kept.
Maintains the TB protocol, schedules annual screening, manages the illness log and exclusions, and requests contractor evidence.
Tracks due dates, collects and files documentation, and keeps medical information confidential.
Send ill employees home, notify the Infection Prevention Coordinator, and do not retaliate against employees who report illness.
Complete screening on time and report symptoms or diagnoses of communicable disease before the next shift.

documentation: TB screening records in the personnel file (initial and annual) and physician or health authority clearance letters
Personnel Compliance Tracker
Employee Illness Log with exclusion and return dates
Contractor TB screening evidence
